On the Average-Case Performance of Greedy
for Maximum Coverage Thanks: Eric Balkanski and Jason Chatzitheodorou were supported in part by NSF grants CCF-2210501 and IIS-2147361.

Eric Balkanski ††thanks: eb3224@columbia.edu Affiliation: Columbia University, IEOR    Jason Chatzitheodorou ††thanks: ic2621@columbia.edu Affiliation: Columbia University, IEOR    Flore Sentenac ††thanks: sentenac@hec.fr Affiliation: HEC Paris, ISOM
Abstract

For the classical maximum coverage problem, the greedy algorithm achieves a worst-case 1−1/e1-1/e approximation, which is optimal unless P=NP\text{P}=\text{NP}. The notion of coverage appears in a wide range of optimization tasks, where empirical evaluations indicate approximation ratios close to 11 for the greedy algorithm on real data. Random models have provided average-case justifications for the empirical performance of many well-known algorithms, but little is known about the average-case performance of greedy for maximum coverage.

We analyze the expected approximation ratio of the greedy algorithm in a random model, which we call the left-regular random model. We first show that, for all parameter settings of this model, the expected approximation ratio of the greedy algorithm improves by a constant over its worst-case 1−1/e1-1/e guarantee. We then identify two simple conditions, either of which ensures that the expected approximation ratio is close to 11 for sufficiently large graphs. Finally, we show that there is a regime where greedy does not achieve an expected approximation better than 0.940.94. To obtain these results, we develop analytical tools, including a novel application of the differential equation method and a connection to maximum matching in Erdős-Rényi graphs, which may be of independent interest for other random models.

1 Introduction

Maximizing coverage is a fundamental problem in computer science and operations research, as the notion of coverage arises across a wide range of optimization tasks. Influence maximization in social networks [18], facility and sensor placement [19], information retrieval [1], content recommendation [26], and finding essential webpages [4] are examples of problems that have been formulated as maximum coverage problems. Maximum coverage is also closely related to set cover, one of Karp’s original 21 NP-complete problems [17].

Maximum coverage can be defined as follows. Given a bipartite graph with left nodes LL and right nodes RR, the goal is to find the kk nodes in LL that cover the largest number of nodes in RR, i.e., maxS⊆L:|S|≤k|N(S)|\max_{S\subseteq L:|S|\leq k}|N(S)|. The greedy algorithm, which iteratively selects the node in LL that covers the largest number of nodes in RR not yet covered, achieves a 1−1/e1-1/e worst-case approximation ratio guarantee [21], which is optimal unless P=NP\text{P}=\text{NP} [11]. However, worst-case guarantees are often driven by pathological instances, leading to pessimistic bounds that can be uninformative in practice. There have been numerous approaches to bridging this gap between theory and practice for various problems through beyond–worst-case analyses of algorithms. A canonical example is the smoothed analysis of the simplex method [27].

For maximum coverage, the greedy algorithm empirically performs significantly better than its 1−1/e1-1/e approximation ratio guarantee [4, 5]. There have been numerous attempts going beyond worst-case to explain this strong performance in practice for the broader problem of monotone submodular maximization under a cardinality constraint. These include the parameterized properties of curvature [8], stability [7], and sharpness [24]. More recently, [25] considered a budget-smoothed model where the cardinality constraint kk is stochastic.

However, except for a few notable exceptions discussed in Section 1.1, little is known about the average-case performance of greedy for maximum coverage on random graphs. In contrast, random models have provided average-case justifications for the performance of classical algorithms such as quicksort [15], first-fit decreasing for bin packing [13], local search for the traveling salesman problem [10], and the greedy algorithm for both max-value [20, 2] and min-cost matching [14]. Motivated by the strong empirical performance of greedy for maximum coverage, we explore the following question.

What is the average-case performance of the greedy algorithm for maximum coverage?

We study the approximation ratio of greedy under a model that we call the left-regular random model LRR​(n,d)\textsc{LRR}(n,d). This model generates a bipartite graph with nn left nodes LL and nn right nodes RR, where each node u∈Lu\in L independently selects dd neighbors uniformly at random from RR. We also consider extensions in which |L|≠|R||L|\neq|R| and the nodes in LL have non-uniform degrees. Our motivation for the dd-regularity assumption for left nodes LL in the base model is that it is a challenging regime for greedy. In particular, there are simple bad instances for greedy in which the left nodes have equal degree (see Section A.1 for an example). Moreover, in empirical evaluations of extensions of this model, greedy’s approximation ratio was lowest when the nodes in LL had equal degree (see Section A.2 for an example).

Our results.

Our first main result is an unconditional bound on the expected approximation ratio of greedy in the left-regular random model. We show that for all values of n,d,n,d, and kk, there is a constant improvement for the approximation ratio of greedy in this random model compared to its worst-case approximation ratio of 1−1/e1-1/e. For all results, we assume that greedy breaks ties according to an arbitrary but consistent ordering of the nodes in LL.

Theorem 1.

There exists a constant c>0c>0 such that for all n∈ℕ,d∈[n],k∈[n]n\in\mathbb{N},d\in[n],k\in[n], the greedy algorithm achieves, in expectation, a (1−1/e+c)(1-1/e+c)-approximation under the left-regular random model.

The second main result provides two alternative sufficient conditions, either of which ensures a near-optimal approximation ratio for greedy for sufficiently large graphs.

Theorem 2.

For any ϵ∈(0,1)\epsilon\in(0,1), n=Ω⁡(ϵ−8)n=\Omega(\epsilon^{-8}), the greedy algorithm achieves, in expectation, a 1−ϵ1-\epsilon approximation under the left-regular random model if either d=Ω⁡(ϵ−8)d=\Omega(\epsilon^{-8}) or k∈[0,ϵ​n2​d]∪[2​nϵ​d,n]k\in\left[0,\frac{\epsilon n}{2d}\right]\cup\left[\frac{2n}{\epsilon d},\,n\right].

This result implies that, for any constant ϵ\epsilon, the degree dd of nodes in LL being super-constant or the cardinality constraint kk lying outside of a constant factor neighborhood of n/dn/d are sufficient conditions for a 1−ϵ1-\epsilon approximation. We note that when k=n/dk=n/d, then the sum of the degrees of kk left nodes is equal to the number of right nodes. The only regime for which Theorem 2 does not give near-optimality is where dd is constant and k=Θ⁡(n/d)k=\Theta(n/d). The third main result shows that for d=2d=2 and some kk such that k=Θ⁡(n/d)k=\Theta(n/d), the approximation ratio of greedy is not near-optimal as nn grows large: it is upper bounded by 0.940.94.

Theorem 3.

For d=2d=2, there exists a sequence k⁡(n)k(n) of cardinality constraints such that the expected approximation ratio of the greedy algorithm is at most 0.940.94 in the limit as n→∞n\rightarrow\infty under the left-regular random model.

These results indicate that the left-regular random model is sufficient to always get a constant improvement in the approximation ratio of greedy, but that it requires additional assumptions for near-optimality; Theorem 2 gives two such assumptions.

Extensions.

We consider two extensions of the left-regular random model.

  • •

    Unbalanced bipartite graphs. We consider an extension ULRR​(n,m,d)\textsc{ULRR}(n,m,d) of the base model LRR​(n,d)\textsc{LRR}(n,d) where the number of right nodes is denoted by mm and is potentially different from the number of left nodes nn. We show that for all n,mn,m such that n=c​mn=cm for some constant c>0c>0 and for all d∈[m]d\in[m] and k∈[n]k\in[n], there exists a constant ϵc>0\epsilon_{c}>0 such that greedy achieves a 1−1/e+ϵc1-1/e+\epsilon_{c} approximation in expectation.

  • •

    Non-regular unbalanced bipartite graphs. We consider an extension GenR​(n,m,{di}i∈[n])\textsc{GenR}(n,m,\{d_{i}\}_{i\in[n]}) of the base model where the left nodes have degree d1≥⋯≥dnd_{1}\geq\cdots\geq d_{n} and the bipartite graph is unbalanced. We show that if either (1) the sum of the kk largest degrees is bounded away from mm: ∑i=1kdi∉[(ϵ/2)​m,(ϵ/2)−1​m]\sum_{i=1}^{k}d_{i}\not\in[(\epsilon/2)m,(\epsilon/2)^{-1}m], (2) the average degree of the kk largest degrees is sufficiently large: 1k​∑i=1kdi=Ω⁡(max⁡(1,(n/m)2)​ϵ−8)\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k}d_{i}=\Omega(\max(1,(n/m)^{2})\epsilon^{-8}), or (3) d1,…,dnd_{1},\ldots,d_{n} are drawn from a power law distribution and kk is sufficiently small, then the expected approximation ratio of greedy is at least 1−ϵ1-\epsilon.

Our techniques.

The positive results rely on two main analytical tools, which may also be of interest for analyzing greedy in other random bipartite graph models.

First, we develop a framework using the differential equation method to analyze an AcceptReject algorithm that is equivalent to greedy. AcceptReject proceeds in phases; in each phase, it iterates through every node to either add it to the solution or reject it. We show that the evolution of the value of the current solution of AcceptReject during the first phase can be approximated by a function that is the unique solution to a differential equation. This differential equation is obtained by approximating the expected per-iteration increase in the solution size as a function of the current solution size.

Second, we show that greedy’s expected value is at least the expected value of a fixed set of kk left nodes, chosen independently of the random graph’s realization. Although this claim may seem intuitive, it requires a careful argument because there are iterations in which the marginal gain of the fixed set is larger than that of greedy, where these marginal gains are measured with respect to their respective current solutions. We circumvent that obstacle by analyzing a hybrid algorithm that runs greedy for tt iterations and then completes the solution by selecting the k−tk-t nodes with the largest residual degrees at iteration tt.

The negative result is established by relating maximum coverage in 22-left regular graphs and maximum matching in Erdős-Rényi random graphs. This connection yields a lower bound on the coverage of the optimal solution via known results on maximum matching. At the same time, we tightly control the performance of greedy through our differential equation analysis.

Open questions.

An alternative random model in which it would be natural to study the approximation ratio of greedy is the Erdős–Rényi random bipartite graph model Gn,n,pG_{n,n,p} with nn left nodes, nn right nodes, and an edge between each left and right node independently with probability pp. To the best of our knowledge, there is no known result for the maximum coverage problem under Erdős–Rényi random bipartite graphs and analyzing greedy in that model seems non-trivial.

Obtaining stronger unconditional bounds on the approximation ratio of greedy in the left-regular random model is a natural direction for future work. In particular, using the differential equation method to analyze additional phases of AcceptReject is a promising direction for establishing stronger approximation guarantees for greedy in the regime where it is not near-optimal.

Paper organization.

We discuss additional related work in Section 1.1 and introduce preliminary definitions and notation in Section 2. In Section 3, we show the approximation guarantees achieved by greedy in the left-regular random model. In Section 4, we show the negative result for greedy. In Appendix E and Appendix F, we study the unbalanced and non-regular extensions of the model.

1.1 Related Work

[4] use the dual of the maximum coverage LP to provide bounds on the approximation ratio of greedy that are in practice much stronger than its worst-case 1−1/e1-1/e approximation. In particular, for k≥50k\geq 50, they obtain bounds on real data that are always at least 0.950.95. They also show that in the random model, where left nodes and right nodes both have degrees that follow a power law distribution and edges are added randomly according to these degree distributions, greedy achieves a 1−ϵ1-\epsilon approximation if it has a marginal contribution of at least O⁡(ϵ−2​log⁡n)O(\epsilon^{-2}\log n) at every iteration. In [28], three algorithms for maximum coverage, including greedy, are analyzed heuristically using the differential equation method on sparse biregular random bipartite graphs. In particular, they use a differential equation to predict a threshold for the cardinality constraint kk below which greedy achieves exact optimality with high probability and above which it is no longer optimal with high probability.

For the closely related set cover problem where the goal is to cover all the nodes in RR with a subset of LL of minimum size, [12] and [6] also study a random model with fixed degrees and also use the differential equation method. However, their primary focus is on methods that, given parameter values for the random model, yield numerical estimates of the approximation ratio of greedy on random instances for these specific parameters, but not closed-form approximation ratios. In addition to these numerical estimates, [12] shows that for a fixed ratio |R|/|L||R|/|L|, greedy is asymptotically optimal as the degree of right nodes tends to infinity. When each edge is included with constant probability, [29] shows that there is an algorithm, distinct from greedy, that is asymptotically optimal for set cover.

2 Preliminaries

In the maximum coverage problem, there is a bipartite graph B=(L,R,E)B=(L,R,E) with nn left nodes L={u1,…,un}L=\{u_{1},\ldots,u_{n}\}, mm right nodes R={v1,…,vm}R=\{v_{1},\ldots,v_{m}\}, and edges E⊆L×RE\subseteq L\times R. The goal is to find the kk nodes in LL that cover the largest number of nodes in RR, i.e., maxS⊆L:|S|≤k|NB(S)|\max_{S\subseteq L:|S|\leq k}|N_{B}(S)| where NB​(S)N_{B}(S) are the neighbors of SS in BB. We abuse notation and write N⁡(S)N(S) when BB is clear from context. The greedy algorithm (Greedy) iteratively adds to the current solution SS the left node that covers the most right nodes not yet covered. We refer to |N⁡(u)∖N⁡(S)||N(u)\setminus N(S)| and |N⁡(S)||N(S)| as the marginal contribution of uu to SS and the value of SS, respectively.

The random graph model.

We consider instances of the maximum coverage problem with random bipartite graphs drawn from the following random graph model that we call the left-regular random model. Throughout the paper, uppercase letters represent fixed sets/graphs, while calligraphic letters denote random sets/graphs.

Definition 1.

The LRR​(n,d)\textsc{LRR}(n,d) model generates a bipartite graph ℬ=(L,R,ℰ)\mathcal{B}=(L,R,\mathcal{E}) by setting |L|=|R|=n|L|=|R|=n and, independently for each u∈Lu\in L, selecting dd neighbors in RR uniformly at random without replacement.

We note that a left-regular random graph satisfies Pr[vj∈N(ui)]=dn\Pr\left[v_{j}\in N(u_{i})\right]=\frac{d}{n} for all vj∈Rv_{j}\in R and ui∈Lu_{i}\in L. When analyzing Greedy under the left-regular random model, we assume it breaks ties according to an arbitrary, but consistent, ordering of the nodes in LL, and that the left nodes uiu_{i} are indexed in the order in which greedy breaks ties.

We let 𝒢k​(ℬ)\mathcal{G}_{k}(\mathcal{B}) and 𝒪k​(ℬ)\mathcal{O}_{k}(\mathcal{B}) denote the greedy solution and the optimal solution, respectively, for the maximum coverage problem with cardinality constraint kk over a bipartite graph ℬ∼LRR​(n,d)\mathcal{B}\sim\textsc{LRR}(n,d). Throughout the paper, approximation guarantees in expectation are defined as ratios of expected values. For fixed n,d,n,d, and kk, the greedy algorithm achieves, in expectation, an α\alpha-approximation if

𝔼ℬ∼LRR​(n,d)⁡[|N⁡(𝒢k​(ℬ))|]≥α⋅𝔼ℬ∼LRR​(n,d)⁡[|N⁡(𝒪k​(ℬ))|].\E\limits_{\mathcal{B}\sim\textsc{LRR}(n,d)}[|N(\mathcal{G}_{k}(\mathcal{B}))|]\geq\alpha\cdot\E\limits_{\mathcal{B}\sim\textsc{LRR}(n,d)}[|N(\mathcal{O}_{k}(\mathcal{B}))|].

We abuse notation and write 𝒢k\mathcal{G}_{k} and 𝒪k\mathcal{O}_{k} when ℬ\mathcal{B} is clear from context. It will be useful in our analysis to compare 𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒢k)|]\E[|N(\mathcal{G}_{k})|] to the expected value of a fixed set of size kk. For that purpose, we denote the first kk left nodes as Hk={u1,u2,…,uk}.H_{k}=\{u_{1},u_{2},\dots,u_{k}\}. We also use the notation [n]={1,…,n}[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}.

3 Approximation Guarantees

In this section, we show that greedy achieves an approximation ratio that is, for all parameters n,dn,d, and kk, a constant improvement over its worst-case 1−1/e1-1/e guarantee and, in a wide range of regimes, asymptotically optimal. We first discuss two central technical tools that we use for these two results in Section 3.1, then partition the space of all parameters in three regions and analyze greedy in each of them in Section 3.2, and finally combine the analyses of these regions to obtain the desired results in Section 3.3. Missing proofs are deferred to Appendix C.

3.1 Technical Tools

The near-linear, saturated, and critical regions.

We distinguish three parameter regimes that we analyze separately. First, for small values of kk, we have the near-linear region, where Greedy selects nodes that have neighborhoods with almost no overlap. Therefore, their value increases almost linearly with kk. Second, for large values of kk, we have the saturated region, where Greedy covers almost all the right nodes. Between these two regions lies the critical region, which is the most challenging to analyze.

The differential equation method.

The first technical tool is a novel application of the differential equation method. We use it to estimate the number of iterations

td=max⁡{t≥1:|N⁡(𝒢t​(ℬ))∖N⁡(𝒢t−1​(ℬ))|=d}t_{d}=\max\{t\geq 1:|N(\mathcal{G}_{t}(\mathcal{B}))\setminus N(\mathcal{G}_{t-1}(\mathcal{B}))|=d\}

in which Greedy, over a left-regular random graph ℬ∼LRR​(n,d)\mathcal{B}\sim\text{{LRR}}(n,d), selects a node with marginal contribution to the current solution 𝒢t−1\mathcal{G}_{t-1} that is equal to dd, i.e., all dd neighbors of the selected node are disjoint from the neighbors of 𝒢t−1\mathcal{G}_{t-1}. The main lemma for this estimate td∗t^{*}_{d} of tdt_{d} is a bound on its error |td−td∗||t_{d}-t^{*}_{d}| that, for any d≤n/2d\leq\sqrt{n/2}, has an O~​(n)\tilde{O}(\sqrt{n}) dependence on nn with high probability.

Lemma 1.

Let n∈ℕn\in\mathbbm{N}, d≤n/2,k∈[n]d\leq\sqrt{n/2},k\in[n] and ℬ∼LRR​(n,d)\mathcal{B}\sim\text{{LRR}}(n,d). With probability at least 1−1n1-\frac{1}{n}, estimate td∗=(1−(1+d⁡(d−1))−1d−1)⋅ndt^{*}_{d}=\left(1-\left(1+d(d-1)\right)^{-\frac{1}{d-1}}\right)\cdot\frac{n}{d} is such that |td−td∗|≤3​ed2⋅8​n​log⁡2​n|t_{d}-t^{*}_{d}|\leq 3e^{d^{2}}\cdot\sqrt{8n\log{2n}}.

This estimate plays a key role in the proof showing that greedy achieves a constant improvement over 1−1/e1-1/e in the critical region when dd is small. To prove Lemma 1, we employ the differential equation method, formalized by [32]. Under appropriate regularity conditions, including bounded increments and Lipschitz continuity, this method yields a high-probability bound on the discrepancy between a discrete stochastic process and the deterministic solution of an associated differential equation. It has found great use in the field of random graphs [12, 23, 32, 31, 20, 3].

We do not apply the method directly to the standard description of Greedy because its evolution is difficult to express through a low-dimensional Markovian state, which is crucial for tractability. Instead, we analyze AcceptReject, an equivalent reformulation of Greedy. AcceptReject, which is formally defined in Algorithm 2, proceeds in phases from p=maxu∈L⁡|N⁡(u)|p=\max_{u\in L}|N(u)| to 11. In phase pp, it iterates over the left nodes uiu_{i} of the bipartite graph in the order in which greedy breaks ties and either accepts (meaning a node gets added to the solution) or rejects each of them based on whether their marginal contribution to the current solution AA is at least pp. This iterative exploration of the graph in each phase implies that its randomness is revealed sequentially, allowing low-dimensional Markovian states to describe the evolution of the current solution size |A||A|.

We denote by 𝒜ip\mathcal{A}^{p}_{i} the set AA of accepted nodes at iteration ii of phase pp of AcceptReject. For the proof of Lemma 1, we focus on analyzing the first phase p=maxu∈L⁡|N⁡(u)|=dp=\max_{u\in L}|N(u)|=d of AcceptReject on a graph ℬ∼LRR​(n,d)\mathcal{B}\sim\text{{LRR}}(n,d).

Proof sketch of Lemma 1 (full proof in Section C.1).

Thus, the number of iterations tdt_{d} where Greedy adds nodes with marginal contribution dd is equal to the number of nodes accepted during the first phase p=dp=d of AcceptReject, i.e., td=|𝒜nd|t_{d}=|\mathcal{A}^{d}_{n}|. We show that 𝒜id\mathcal{A}^{d}_{i} and FF satisfy these four conditions with parameters such that the resulting approximation td=|𝒜nd|≈n⋅y⁡(1)t_{d}=|\mathcal{A}^{d}_{n}|\approx n\cdot y(1) is sufficiently tight to imply the desired bound. ∎

A promising direction for future work is to leverage estimates of the number of accepts across all phases, rather than only the first, as this could yield a tighter lower bound on the coverage of Greedy. The main challenge is that the solution of the differential equations in each phase depends on the solutions from the preceding phases, making closed-form expressions analogous to those obtained for tdt_{d} unlikely. This interdependence substantially complicates the derivation of the approximation ratio. Nevertheless, we believe that a sufficiently careful analysis could overcome these technical obstacles and uncover the true extent of the improvement that Greedy achieves over 1−1/e1-1/e.

The fixed-set lower bound.

The second technical tool provides a seemingly simple lower bound on the expected value of the greedy solution. The lower bound is the expected value of a fixed set of left nodes chosen independently of the realization of the random graph. For this fixed set of nodes, we consider the kk nodes with lowest indices Hk={u1,…,uk}H_{k}=\{u_{1},\dots,u_{k}\}.

Lemma 2.

Let n∈ℕn\in\mathbbm{N}, d∈[n],k∈[n]d\in[n],k\in[n], and ℬ∼LRR​(n,d)\mathcal{B}\sim\text{{LRR}}(n,d), then 𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒢k)|]≥𝔼⁡[|N⁡(Hk)|]\E\left[|N(\mathcal{G}_{k})|\right]\geq\E\left[|N(H_{k})|\right].

In Section 3.2, we use this bound to show that greedy is near-optimal in the near-linear, the saturated, and the critical region when dd is large. The only region where it does not provide a constant improvement is in the critical region when dd is small, where we use Lemma 1 instead.

It may seem natural that Greedy performs better than HkH_{k} over left-regular random graphs. However, a difficulty that arises in proving Lemma 2, is that the expected marginal improvement 𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒢t)∖N⁡(𝒢t−1)|]\E[|N(\mathcal{G}_{t})\setminus N(\mathcal{G}_{t-1})|] of Greedy is not always larger than the expected marginal improvement 𝔼⁡[|N⁡(Ht)∖N⁡(Ht−1)|]\E[|N(H_{t})\setminus N(H_{t-1})|] of HkH_{k} at all iterations tt, which we illustrate in Fig. 2 in Section C.1. Nevertheless, in the early iterations, where a small number of right nodes have been covered, it does hold that 𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒢t)∖N⁡(𝒢t−1)|]≥𝔼⁡[|N⁡(Ht)∖N⁡(Ht−1)|]\E[|N(\mathcal{G}_{t})\setminus N(\mathcal{G}_{t-1})|]\geq\E[|N(H_{t})\setminus N(H_{t-1})|]. The challenge is thus to show that the expected value of Greedy remains larger in later iterations.

Proof sketch of Lemma 2 (full proof in Section C.1).

We define a hybrid algorithm 𝒴t\mathcal{Y}^{t} that runs in two phases. First, it runs tt iterations of Greedy, after which its current solution is 𝒢t\mathcal{G}_{t}. In the second phase, it adds to the solution the k−tk-t nodes with largest marginal contribution to 𝒢t\mathcal{G}_{t}.

The main part of the proof consists in showing that trading one iteration of Greedy in the first phase for one more node in the second phase reduces the expected value, i.e.,

𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒴t)|]≥𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒴t−1)|].\E\left[|N(\mathcal{Y}^{t})|\right]\geq\E\left[|N(\mathcal{Y}^{t-1})|\right].

To show that inequality, we first note that 𝒢t⊆𝒴t∩𝒴t−1\mathcal{G}_{t}\subseteq\mathcal{Y}^{t}\cap\mathcal{Y}^{t-1}, which implies that it suffices to compare the marginal contribution of the k−tk-t other nodes in the two solutions to 𝒢t\mathcal{G}_{t}. The crucial difference that we leverage is that the k−tk-t other nodes in 𝒴t\mathcal{Y}^{t} are selected to be the nodes with largest marginal contribution to 𝒢t\mathcal{G}_{t}, whereas for 𝒴t−1\mathcal{Y}^{t-1} they are the nodes with largest marginal contribution to 𝒢t−1\mathcal{G}_{t-1}. With 𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒴t)|]≥𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒴t−1)|],\E\left[|N(\mathcal{Y}^{t})|\right]\geq\E\left[|N(\mathcal{Y}^{t-1})|\right], the lemma then follows since 𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒢k)|]=𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒴k)|]\E\left[|N(\mathcal{G}_{k})|\right]=\E\left[|N(\mathcal{Y}^{k})|\right] and 𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒴0)|]=𝔼⁡[|N⁡(Hk)|].\E\left[|N(\mathcal{Y}^{0})|\right]=\E\left[|N(H_{k})|\right]. ∎

3.2 Analysis For The Different Regions

Near-linear and saturated regions.

In both regions, we show that Greedy achieves a ratio close to 11 in Lemma 3. Intuitively, in the near-linear region (i.e., k<<n/dk<<n/d), even the nodes of HkH_{k} share very few neighbors; therefore, the expected value of Greedy is close to k​dkd. On the other hand, in the saturated region (i.e., k>>n/dk>>n/d), HkH_{k} covers most of the right nodes, even if the nodes of HkH_{k} share many neighbors.

Lemma 3.

Let ϵ∈(0,1),n∈ℕ,d∈[n],k∈[0,ϵ​n2​d]∪[2​nϵ​d,n]\epsilon\in(0,1),n\in\mathbbm{N},d\in[n],k\in\left[0,\frac{\epsilon n}{2d}\right]\cup[\frac{2n}{\epsilon d},n] and ℬ∼LRR​(n,d)\mathcal{B}\sim\text{{LRR}}(n,d). Then we have 𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒢k)|]≥(1−ϵ)⋅𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒪k)|]\E\left[|N(\mathcal{G}_{k})|\right]\geq\left(1-\epsilon\right)\cdot\E\left[|N(\mathcal{O}_{k})|\right].

The proof uses the fixed set lower bound from Lemma 2, whose value is lower bounded by the following lemma (proof deferred to Section C.1).

Lemma 4.

Let n∈ℕn\in\mathbbm{N}, d∈[n],k∈[n]d\in[n],k\in[n], and ℬ∼LRR​(n,d)\mathcal{B}\sim\text{{LRR}}(n,d). Then 𝔼⁡[|N⁡(Hk)|]≥(1−e−kdn)⋅n\E\left[|N(H_{k})|\right]\geq\left(1-e^{-\frac{kd}{n}}\right)\cdot n.

The proof also uses the following inequality, whose proof is deferred to Section C.2.

Claim 1.

For all ϵ∈(0,1)\epsilon\in(0,1), 1−e−ϵϵ≥1−ϵ\frac{1-e^{-\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\geq 1-\epsilon.

We are now ready to prove Lemma 3.

Proof of Lemma 3.

For k≥2​nϵ​dk\geq\frac{2n}{\epsilon d}:

𝔼[|N(𝒢k)|]≥𝔼[|N(Hk)|]≥(1−e−kd/n)n≥(1−e−1/ϵ)⋅n≥(1−ϵ)⋅𝔼[|N(𝒪k)|],\displaystyle\E\left[|N(\mathcal{G}_{k})|\right]\geq\E\left[|N(H_{k})|\right]\geq\left(1-e^{-kd/n}\right)n\geq\left(1-e^{-1/\epsilon}\right)\cdot n\geq\left(1-\epsilon\right)\cdot\E\left[|N(\mathcal{O}_{k})|\right],

where the first inequality is because 𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒢k)|]\E\left[|N(\mathcal{G}_{k})|\right] is lower bounded by 𝔼⁡[|N⁡(Hk)|]\E\left[|N(H_{k})|\right] by Lemma 2, the second inequality is due to Lemma 4, the third inequality is because k​d/n≥2/ϵ≥1/ϵkd/n\geq 2/\epsilon\geq 1/\epsilon by assumption, the fourth inequality is due to e−1/ϵ≤ϵe^{-1/\epsilon}\leq\epsilon and |N⁡(𝒪k)||N(\mathcal{O}_{k})| is upper bounded by nn. For k≤ϵ​n2​dk\leq\frac{\epsilon n}{2d}:

𝔼[|N(𝒢k)|]≥𝔼[|N(Hk)|]≥(−e−kd/n)n=1−e−kd/nkd/n⋅kd≥−e−ϵϵ⋅kd≥(−ϵ)⋅𝔼[|N(𝒪k)|],\displaystyle\E\left[|N(\mathcal{G}_{k})|\right]\geq\E\left[|N(H_{k})|\right]\geq\left(1\!-\!e^{-kd/n}\right)n=\frac{1-e^{-kd/n}}{kd/n}\cdot kd\geq\frac{1\!-\!e^{-\epsilon}}{\epsilon}\cdot kd\geq\left(1\!-\!\epsilon\right)\cdot\E\left[|N(\mathcal{O}_{k})|\right],

where the first inequality is because 𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒢k)|]\E\left[|N(\mathcal{G}_{k})|\right] is lower bounded by 𝔼⁡[|N⁡(Hk)|]\E\left[|N(H_{k})|\right] by Lemma 2, the second inequality is due to Lemma 4, the third inequality is because k​d/n≤ϵ/2≤ϵkd/n\leq\epsilon/2\leq\epsilon by assumption, the fourth inequality is due to Claim 1 and |N⁡(𝒪k)||N(\mathcal{O}_{k})| is upper bounded by k​dkd. ∎

Critical region: large degrees.

We use Lemma 2 and Chernoff bounds over negatively correlated variables to show a 1−ϵ1-\epsilon ratio in the critical region (i.e. k≈n/dk\approx n/d) when the degrees are large. Intuitively, it is possible to upper bound the optimal solution, since any kk nodes suffer from sharing too many neighbors.

Lemma 5.

Let ϵ∈(0,1),d≥204ϵ8,n≥d,k∈[ϵ​n2​d,2​nϵ​d],\epsilon\in(0,1),d\geq\frac{20^{4}}{\epsilon^{8}},n\geq d,k\in\left[\frac{\epsilon n}{2d},\frac{2n}{\epsilon d}\right], and ℬ∼LRR​(n,d)\mathcal{B}\sim\text{{LRR}}(n,d). Then we have 𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒢k)|]≥(1−ϵ)⋅𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒪k)|]\E\left[|N(\mathcal{G}_{k})|\right]\geq\left(1-\epsilon\right)\cdot\E\left[|N(\mathcal{O}_{k})|\right].

Proof sketch (full proof in Section C.2).

We show that the values of all sets concentrate with high probability. To this end, we express the value |N(S)|=∑v∈R𝟙{v∈N(S)}|N(S)|=\sum_{v\in R}\mathbbm{1}\{v\in N(S)\} of a set SS as the sum over v∈Rv\in R of the indicator variables for whether vv is covered by SS. We first show that these indicator variables are negatively correlated.

We then use a generalization of the Chernoff bound for negatively correlated variables and a union bound to show that Pr[|N(𝒪k)|≥(1+δ)⋅𝔼[|N(Hk)|]]≤1n\Pr\left[|N(\mathcal{O}_{k})|\geq(1+\delta)\cdot\E\left[|N(H_{k})|\right]\right]\leq\frac{1}{n} for an appropriate choice of δ\delta. It then follows that 𝔼[|N(𝒢k)|]≥𝔼[|N(Hk)|]≥11+ϵ𝔼[|N(𝒪k)]\E\left[|N(\mathcal{G}_{k})|\right]\geq\E\left[|N(H_{k})|\right]\geq\frac{1}{1+\epsilon}\E\left[|N(\mathcal{O}_{k})\right], where the first inequality is by Lemma 2 and the second inequality by the choice of δ\delta and the assumption on nn. ∎

Critical region: small degrees.

We use Lemma 1 to lower bound the ratio in the critical region, when the degrees are small. The main challenge in this case is that the optimal solution can achieve a high value close to nn, so Lemmas 2 and 4 only retrieve worst-case ratio 1−1e1-\frac{1}{e}. Therefore, we need a tighter lower bound for Greedy. This is the most challenging case and the only one in which we do not show a 1−ϵ1-\epsilon ratio. Nevertheless, we still improve over the 1−1e1-\frac{1}{e} ratio by a constant, albeit small.

Lemma 6.

There exists a function n0​(x):(0,1)→ℕn_{0}(x):(0,1)\rightarrow\mathbbm{N} such that for ϵ∈(0,1),n≥n0​(ϵ),d≤204ϵ8,k∈[ϵ​n2​d,2​nϵ​d],\epsilon\in(0,1),n\geq n_{0}(\epsilon),d\leq\frac{20^{4}}{\epsilon^{8}},k\in\left[\frac{\epsilon n}{2d},\frac{2n}{\epsilon d}\right], and ℬ∼LRR​(n,d)\mathcal{B}\sim\text{{LRR}}(n,d), we have 𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒢k)|]≥(1−1e+Ω⁡(ϵ24))⋅𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒪k)|]\E\left[|N(\mathcal{G}_{k})|\right]\geq\left(1-\frac{1}{e}+\Omega\left(\epsilon^{24}\right)\right)\cdot\E\left[|N(\mathcal{O}_{k})|\right].

The proof uses worst-case analysis after iteration tdt_{d}, to obtain a result for k≥tdk\geq t_{d}. Specifically, we show that as long as tdt_{d} is on the order of n/dn/d, Greedy is bounded a constant away from 1−1e1-\frac{1}{e}, which we formalize in the following lemma.

Lemma 7.

Let B=(L,R,E)B=(L,R,E) be a dd-left-regular bipartite graph with |L|=|R|=n|L|=|R|=n. For all k≥tdk\geq t_{d} we have |N⁡(Gk)|≥(1−1e+1e⋅(tdn/d)3)⋅|N⁡(Ok)||N(G_{k})|\geq\left(1-\frac{1}{e}+\frac{1}{e}\cdot\left(\frac{t_{d}}{n/d}\right)^{3}\right)\cdot|N(O_{k})|.

We are now ready to give a proof sketch of Lemma 6.

Proof sketch of Lemma 6 (full proof in Section C.2).

Let δ\delta be an appropriately chosen error term. For k≤td∗−δk\leq t^{*}_{d}-\delta, Greedy gains dd on each iteration with high probability by Lemma 1, so 𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒢k)|]≥(1−1n)⋅𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒪k)|].\E\left[|N(\mathcal{G}_{k})|\right]\geq\left(1-\frac{1}{n}\right)\cdot\E\left[|N(\mathcal{O}_{k})|\right]. For k≥td∗−δk\geq t^{*}_{d}-\delta, Greedy gains dd on each iteration until td∗−δt^{*}_{d}-\delta with high probability by Lemma 1, and for later iterations we use Lemma 7:

𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒢k)|]≥(1−1e+1e⋅(td∗−δn/d)3−8ϵ​n)⋅𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒪k)|].\displaystyle\E\left[|N(\mathcal{G}_{k})|\right]\geq\left(1-\frac{1}{e}+\frac{1}{e}\cdot\left(\frac{t^{*}_{d}-\delta}{n/d}\right)^{3}-\frac{8}{\epsilon n}\right)\cdot\E\left[|N(\mathcal{O}_{k})|\right].

We choose n0​(ϵ)n_{0}(\epsilon) large enough to make terms δn/d=O⁡(ϵ8)\frac{\delta}{n/d}=O(\epsilon^{8}) and 8ϵ​n=O⁡(ϵ25)\frac{8}{\epsilon n}=O(\epsilon^{25}). The statement follows by lower bounding td∗−δn/d=Ω⁡(ϵ8)\frac{t^{*}_{d}-\delta}{n/d}=\Omega(\epsilon^{8}). ∎

3.3 Putting Everything Together

By combining Lemma 3 and Lemma 5, we immediately get the near-optimality of greedy in the near-linear region, saturated region, and critical region with large degrees. See 2

The second main result regarding the approximation guarantee of greedy requires the following inequality (proof in Section C.2).

Claim 2.

For all k≥1k\geq 1, (1−1k)k≤1e−14​e​k\left(1-\frac{1}{k}\right)^{k}\leq\frac{1}{e}-\frac{1}{4ek}.

By combining Lemma 6, which is for the critical region with small degrees, and Theorem 2, which is for all other regions, we get the constant improvement over 1−1/e1-1/e for all regions.

See 1

Proof.

Let ϵ=0.3\epsilon=0.3 and n0​(x)n_{0}(x) be the function from the statement of Lemma 6. For n≥n0​(ϵ)n\geq n_{0}(\epsilon), the statement is implied by Theorems 2 and 6. For n<n0​(ϵ)n<n_{0}(\epsilon), the worst-case approximation ratio of greedy is 1−(1−1k)k1-\left(1-\frac{1}{k}\right)^{k}, so we get

1−(1−1k)k≥1−1e+14​e​k≥1−1e+14​e​n0​(ϵ),\displaystyle 1-\left(1-\frac{1}{k}\right)^{k}\geq 1-\frac{1}{e}+\frac{1}{4ek}\geq 1-\frac{1}{e}+\frac{1}{4en_{0}(\epsilon)},

4 Limitation of Greedy

In the previous section, Theorem 2 does not guarantee an approximation ratio close to 11 for all parameter values. The remaining difficult regime is when the degree dd is small and kk lies in a critical window around n/dn/d. In this section, we establish Theorem 3, which demonstrates that this gap is due to a fundamental limitation of Greedy rather than a proof artifact. Specifically, we identify a counterexample with d=2d=2, where the ratio is bounded away from 11 as nn goes to infinity. The main results are Lemmas 9 and 11, which lower bound Opt and upper bound Greedy respectively. We defer the complete proofs to Appendix D.

4.1 Lower Bound for Opt

The first challenge is to lower-bound the value of the optimal solution. We resolve this difficulty by relating the value of the optimal solution in 22-left-regular random graphs to the size of a maximum matching in Erdős-Renyi random graphs. This process takes two steps.

First, the value of the optimal solution in any 22-left-regular bipartite graph B=(L,R,E)B=(L,R,E) is at least twice the minimum between kk and the size of the largest set of left nodes with no common neighbors, i.e.

|N⁡(𝒪k​(B))|≥2​min⁡(k,λ⁡(B)),\displaystyle|N(\mathcal{O}_{k}(B))|\geq 2\min\left(k,\lambda(B)\right), (1)

with

λ⁡(B)=max⁡{|S|:S⊆L​ s.t. ​N​(u)∩N⁡(u′)=∅​∀u≠u′∈S}.\displaystyle\lambda(B)=\max\{|S|:S\subseteq L\text{ s.t. }N(u)\cap N(u^{\prime})=\emptyset\ \forall u\neq u^{\prime}\in S\}. (2)

The following lemma reduces the computation of λ⁡(B)\lambda(B) to finding the size of a maximum matching in a specific graph IBI_{B}, defined as follows: the vertex set of IBI_{B} is the set of right nodes of BB, and for each left node u∈Lu\in L, we add an edge in IBI_{B} between the two neighbors of uu. If two nodes on the left side share the same neighbor set, the parallel edges are merged; in other words, IBI_{B} is a simple graph.

Lemma 8.

Let B=(L,R,E)B=(L,R,E) be a 22-left-regular bipartite graph. Also let IB=(R,EB)I_{B}=(R,E_{B}) be a graph such that EB={e1,…,en}E_{B}=\{e_{1},\dots,e_{n}\} where ei=N⁡(ui)e_{i}=N(u_{i}) for all i∈[n]i\in[n]. Then λ⁡(B)=μ⁡(IB)\lambda(B)=\mu(I_{B}), where μ⁡(IB)\mu(I_{B}) is the size of the maximum matching in IBI_{B}.

Proof.

Consider a set S⊆LS\subseteq L attaining the maximum in Equation (2), i.e., |S|=λ⁡(B)|S|=\lambda(B) and N⁡(u)∩N⁡(u′)=∅N(u)\cap N(u^{\prime})=\emptyset for all distinct u,u′∈Su,u^{\prime}\in S. We construct

M={ei:ui∈S},M=\{e_{i}:u_{i}\in S\},

which is a valid matching in IBI_{B} by definition of SS, and clearly |M|=|S||M|=|S|. We now show that MM is a maximum matching in IBI_{B}. Towards a contradiction, assume there exists a matching M′M^{\prime} in IBI_{B} such that |M′|>|M||M^{\prime}|>|M|. Then we can define:

S′={ui:ei∈M′},\displaystyle S^{\prime}=\{u_{i}:e_{i}\in M^{\prime}\},

where N⁡(ui)∩N⁡(uj)=∅N(u_{i})\cap N(u_{j})=\emptyset for all ui,uj∈S′u_{i},u_{j}\in S^{\prime} since M′M^{\prime} is a matching. Then |S′|=|M′|>|M|=|S|=λ⁡(B)|S^{\prime}|=|M^{\prime}|>|M|=|S|=\lambda(B), which contradicts optimality of SS. The statement follows as λ⁡(B)=|S|=|M|=μ⁡(IB)\lambda(B)=|S|=|M|=\mu(I_{B}). ∎

Now suppose that ℬ\mathcal{B} is sampled from LRR​(n,2)\text{{LRR}}(n,2). Then ℐℬ\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{B}} is distributed as a graph on nn vertices obtained by sampling nn edges independently and uniformly at random with replacement from the (n2)\binom{n}{2} possible edges, merging parallel edges. This distribution is closely related to the classical Erdős–Rényi model 𝔾n,m\mathbbm{G}_{n,m}, in which mm edges are sampled uniformly at random without replacement. Sharp estimates for the maximum matching size in Erdős–Rényi graphs are known; see, e.g., [16]. As we show in the following lemma, these results yield a bound on μ⁡(ℐℬ)\mu(\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{B}}), which can be translated into a lower bound on the expected value of the optimal solution. Before we proceed, we define constants γ∗,γ∗\gamma_{*},\gamma^{*}, where γ∗\gamma_{*} is the smallest root of x=2​e−2​e−xx=2e^{-2e^{-x}} and γ∗=2​e−γ∗\gamma^{*}=2e^{-\gamma_{*}} since we use them extensively in our proofs.

Lemma 9.

Let n∈ℕn\in\mathbbm{N} and ℬ∼LRR​(n,2)\mathcal{B}\sim\text{{LRR}}\left(n,2\right). Then for any k≤(1−γ∗+γ∗+γ∗​γ∗4−n−19)⋅nk\leq\left(1-\frac{\gamma^{*}+\gamma_{*}+\gamma^{*}\gamma_{*}}{4}-n^{-\frac{1}{9}}\right)\cdot n, we have 𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒪k)|]≥(1−o⁡(1))⋅2​k.\E\left[|N(\mathcal{O}_{k})|\right]\geq(1-o(1))\cdot 2k.

The proof leverages the following lemma, which provides a probabilistic lower bound on the size of the maximum matching in ℐℬ\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{B}}.

Lemma 10.

Let n∈ℕn\in\mathbbm{N} and ℬ∼LRR​(n,2)\mathcal{B}\sim\text{{LRR}}\left(n,2\right), then

Pr[μ(ℐℬ)≥(1−γ∗+γ∗+γ∗​γ∗4−n−19)⋅n]≥1−o(1).\Pr\left[\mu(\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{B}})\geq\left(1-\frac{\gamma^{*}+\gamma_{*}+\gamma^{*}\gamma_{*}}{4}-n^{-\frac{1}{9}}\right)\cdot n\right]\geq 1-o(1).

The proof, deferred to Appendix D, bounds how much the maximum matching size can change due to the discrepancy between the generation process of ℐℬ\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{B}} and the seminal Erdős-Renyi model, and leverages what is known about the size of maximum matchings in Erdős-Renyi. We are now ready to prove Lemma 9.

Proof of Lemma 9.

Consider any k≤(1−γ∗+γ∗+γ∗​γ∗4−n−19)⋅nk\leq\left(1-\frac{\gamma^{*}+\gamma_{*}+\gamma^{*}\gamma_{*}}{4}-n^{-\frac{1}{9}}\right)\cdot n, then:

𝔼[|N(𝒪k)|]≥2k⋅Pr[λ(ℬ)≥k]=2k⋅Pr[μ(ℐℬ)≥k],\displaystyle\E\left[|N(\mathcal{O}_{k})|\right]\geq 2k\cdot\Pr\left[\lambda(\mathcal{B})\geq k\right]=2k\cdot\Pr\left[\mu(\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{B}})\geq k\right],

where the inequality is due to Eq. 1 and the equality is due to λ⁡(ℬ)=μ⁡(ℐℬ)\lambda(\mathcal{B})=\mu(\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{B}}) by Lemma 8. We now lower bound μ⁡(ℐℬ)\mu(\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{B}}):

Pr[μ(ℐℬ)≥k]≥Pr[μ(ℐℬ)≥(1−γ∗+γ∗+γ∗​γ∗4−n−19)⋅n]≥1−o(1),\displaystyle\Pr\left[\mu(\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{B}})\geq k\right]\geq\Pr\left[\mu(\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{B}})\geq\left(1-\frac{\gamma^{*}+\gamma_{*}+\gamma^{*}\gamma_{*}}{4}-n^{-\frac{1}{9}}\right)\cdot n\right]\geq 1-o(1),

where the first inequality is due to the assumption on kk and the second due to Lemma 10. Chaining with the previous inequality establishes the lemma. ∎

4.2 Upper Bound for Greedy

The second challenge is to upper bound the value of Greedy. We do so through the machinery of Lemma 1 in the following lemma.

Lemma 11.

Let n∈ℕn\in\mathbbm{N} and ℬ∼LRR​(n,2)\mathcal{B}\sim\text{{LRR}}\left(n,2\right). Then we have that, for any k>13⋅nk>\frac{1}{3}\cdot n, 𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒢k)|]≤(1+o⁡(1))⋅(13⋅n+k)\E\left[|N(\mathcal{G}_{k})|\right]\leq(1+o(1))\cdot\left(\frac{1}{3}\cdot n+k\right).

Proof.

By definition of t2t_{2}, up to iteration t2t_{2}, Greedy will gain 22 per iteration, and thereafter it gains at most 11 per iteration. Consequently, for any kk, the following holds

𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒢k)|]≤𝔼⁡[2​t2+(k−t2)]=𝔼⁡[t2]+k.\mathbb{E}\left[|N(\mathcal{G}_{k})|\right]\leq\mathbb{E}\left[2t_{2}+(k-t_{2})\right]=\mathbb{E}[t_{2}]+k.

As t2≤nt_{2}\leq n always holds, we have:

𝔼[t2]≤t2∗+3e4⋅8​n​log⁡2​n+n⋅Pr[t2≥t2∗+3e4⋅8​n​log⁡2​n].\mathbb{E}[t_{2}]\leq t^{*}_{2}+3e^{4}\cdot\sqrt{8n\log{2n}}+n\cdot\Pr\left[t_{2}\geq t^{*}_{2}+3e^{4}\cdot\sqrt{8n\log{2n}}\right].

We upper bound the probability using Lemma 1:

Pr[t2≥t2∗+3e4⋅8​n​log⁡2​n]≤1n.\Pr\left[t_{2}\geq t^{*}_{2}+3e^{4}\cdot\sqrt{8n\log{2n}}\right]\leq\frac{1}{n}.

Chaining those three inequalities yields:

𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒢k)|]≤t2∗+3​e4⋅8​n​log⁡2​n+1+k=(1+3​e4⋅8​n​log⁡2​n+1t2∗+k)​(t2∗+k).\mathbb{E}\left[|N(\mathcal{G}_{k})|\right]\leq t^{*}_{2}+3e^{4}\cdot\sqrt{8n\log{2n}}+1+k=\left(1+\frac{3e^{4}\cdot\sqrt{8n\log{2n}}+1}{t^{*}_{2}+k}\right)(t^{*}_{2}+k).

The statement then follows, since t2∗=n/3t^{*}_{2}=n/3 by definition. ∎

4.3 Putting Everything Together

We proceed to show Theorem 3 by combining Lemmas 9 and 11. See 3

Proof.

Let k⁡(n)=⌊(1−γ∗+γ∗+γ∗​γ∗4−n−19)⋅n⌋k(n)=\left\lfloor\left(1-\frac{\gamma^{*}+\gamma_{*}+\gamma^{*}\gamma_{*}}{4}-n^{-\frac{1}{9}}\right)\cdot n\right\rfloor, then we have:

Appendix A Additional Discussion about the Left-Regular Random Model

A.1 A Simple Bad Instance for Greedy over a Left-Regular Graph

The following instance corresponds to the classical bad instance for greedy originally provided in [22] to show that greedy achieves at best a 1−1/e1-1/e approximation, as described using the notation from [24]. We highlight that this simple and original instance from [22] is left-regular with all the left nodes having equal degree. The instance is the following

  • •

    cardinality constraint kk,

  • •

    right nodes R={1,…,k}kR=\{1,\ldots,k\}^{k} with |R|=kk|R|=k^{k},

  • •

    left nodes L={a1,…,ak−1}∪{b1,…,bk}L=\{a_{1},\ldots,a_{k-1}\}\cup\{b_{1},\ldots,b_{k}\} with

    • –

      N⁡(ai)={x∈R:xi=1}N(a_{i})=\{x\in R:x_{i}=1\} for i∈[k−1]i\in[k-1], and

    • –

      N⁡(bi)={x∈R:xk=i}N(b_{i})=\{x\in R:x_{k}=i\} for i∈[k]i\in[k]

We note that this graph is left-regular with all the nodes in LL having degree kk−1k^{k-1}. The optimal solution is {b1,…,bk}\{b_{1},\ldots,b_{k}\}, which covers all the right nodes and thus has value kkk^{k}. Note that for any S⊆{a1,…,ak−1}S\subseteq\{a_{1},\ldots,a_{k-1}\}, the marginal contribution of each node u∈L∖Su\in L\setminus S to SS is identical and equal to 1k⋅|R∖N⁡(S)|\frac{1}{k}\cdot|R\setminus N(S)|, i.e., a 1/k1/k fraction of the right nodes not covered by SS. If greedy breaks ties according to order (a1,…,ak−1,b1,…,bk)(a_{1},\ldots,a_{k-1},b_{1},\ldots,b_{k}), it returns solution {a1,…,ak−1,b1}\{a_{1},\ldots,a_{k-1},b_{1}\}, which has value

(1−(1−1k)k)​|R|,\left(1-\left(1-\frac{1}{k}\right)^{k}\right)|R|,

whose limit approaches 1−1/e1-1/e as kk grows large. This bipartite graph can of course be made balanced with |L|=|R||L|=|R| by adding a sufficient number of copies of an arbitrary left node.

A.2 Empirical Performance of Greedy over Random Graphs with Uneven Left-Node Degrees

We evaluate Greedy over random graphs with left nodes whose degrees are either equal or have different level of unevenness. We use this family of instances as an example to illustrate that, for random graphs and at least experimentally, greedy seems to perform worse when the degrees of the left nodes are all equal.

To make the comparison clear, we use parameter a∈[0,1]a\in[0,1] to interpolate between equal degrees (a=0a=0) and unequal degrees (a=1a=1), while keeping the average degree fixed. The instances we create for our experiments have left degrees randomly chosen from 1,4,71,4,7 with probabilities a2,1−a,a2\frac{a}{2},1-a,\frac{a}{2}, so that the average degree is always 44. For each value of aa, we estimate:

mink∈[n]⁡𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒢k)|]𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒪k)|].\displaystyle\min_{k\in[n]}\frac{\E\left[|N(\mathcal{G}_{k})|\right]}{\E\left[|N(\mathcal{O}_{k})|\right]}.

As we can see in Fig. 1, the lowest ratio is achieved for equal degrees (a=0a=0).

Appendix B Generalization Of Technical Tools

In this section, we show that our main techniques from the proof of Theorems 1 and 2, can be used in a more general random model that allows different number of nodes on each side of the bipartite graph as well as non-uniform degrees for the left nodes.

Definition 2.

Let n,m∈ℕn,m\in\mathbbm{N} and d∈[m]d\in[m]. The random model GenR(n,m,d1,…,dnn,m,d_{1},\dots,d_{n}) constructs a random bipartite graph ℬ=(L,R,ℰ)\mathcal{B}=\left(L,R,\mathcal{E}\right) such that the number of nodes is |L|=n,|R|=m|L|=n,|R|=m and the edges ℰ\mathcal{E} are such that N⁡(ui)∈(Rdi)N(u_{i})\in\binom{R}{d_{i}} is selected uniformly and independently for all i∈[n]i\in[n].

Notice that, GenR generalizes LRR and ULRR.

B.1.1 Number of accepts in first phase

In the following lemma we calculate the accepts of phase 1 by using the differential equation method.

Let n,m∈ℕn,m\in\mathbbm{N}, d∈[m],k∈[n]d\in[m],k\in[n] and draw bipartite graph ℬ=(L,R,ℰ)\mathcal{B}=(L,R,\mathcal{E}) from random model GenR​(n,m,d,…,d)\textsc{GenR}(n,m,d,\dots,d). Then |td−td∗|≤δ|t_{d}-t^{*}_{d}|\leq\delta with probability at 1−1n1-\frac{1}{n} for all m≥2​d2m\geq 2d^{2}.

Due to the equivalence between AcceptReject and Greedy Lemma 12, on any graph B=(L,R,E)B=(L,R,E) we have td=|𝒜nd|t_{d}=|\mathcal{A}^{d}_{n}|, since at the end of phase dd, AcceptReject has accepted all the nodes with marginal contribution dd. y′​(t)=(1−n​dm⋅y⁡(t))d,y⁡(0)=0.\displaystyle y^{\prime}(t)=\left(1-\frac{nd}{m}\cdot y(t)\right)^{d},\ y(0)=0.

|Y⁡(i)−n​y​(i/n)|<3​en​d2m​T⋅λ​n=3​en​d2m⋅8​n​log⁡(2​n).\displaystyle\bigl|Y(i)-ny(i/n)\bigr|<3e^{\frac{nd^{2}}{m}T}\cdot\lambda n=3e^{\frac{nd^{2}}{m}}\cdot\sqrt{8n\log(2n)}.

∎

In the following lemma we approximate the probability of success.

Lemma 14.

Let d∈ℕd\in\mathbbm{N}, m≥2​d2m\geq 2d^{2}, r∈[m]r\in[m] then |(rd)/(md)−(rm)d|≤2​d2m|\binom{r}{d}/\binom{m}{d}-\left(\frac{r}{m}\right)^{d}|\leq\frac{2d^{2}}{m}.

(rd)(md)=r(r−1)⋯(r−d+1))m(m−1)⋯(m−d+1)=∏i=0d−1(r−im−i)≤(rm)d.\displaystyle\frac{\binom{r}{d}}{\binom{m}{d}}=\frac{r(r-1)\cdots(r-d+1))}{m(m-1)\cdots(m-d+1)}=\prod_{i=0}^{d-1}\left(\frac{r-i}{m-i}\right)\leq\left(\frac{r}{m}\right)^{d}.

≥(rm)d⋅(1−∑i=0d−1i⁡(m−r)r⁡(m−i))\displaystyle\geq\left(\frac{r}{m}\right)^{d}\cdot\left(1-\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}\frac{i(m-r)}{r(m-i)}\right)
≥(rm)d⋅(1−m−rr⁡(m−d)⋅∑i=0d−1i)\displaystyle\geq\left(\frac{r}{m}\right)^{d}\cdot\left(1-\frac{m-r}{r(m-d)}\cdot\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}i\right)
=(rm)d⋅(1−m−rr⁡(m−d)⋅d⁡(d−1)2)\displaystyle=\left(\frac{r}{m}\right)^{d}\cdot\left(1-\frac{m-r}{r(m-d)}\cdot\frac{d(d-1)}{2}\right)
=(rm)d−(rm)d−1⋅m−rm−d⋅d22​m\displaystyle=\left(\frac{r}{m}\right)^{d}-\left(\frac{r}{m}\right)^{d-1}\cdot\frac{m-r}{m-d}\cdot\frac{d^{2}}{2m}
≥(rm)d−mm−d⋅d22​m\displaystyle\geq\left(\frac{r}{m}\right)^{d}-\frac{m}{m-d}\cdot\frac{d^{2}}{2m}
≥(rm)d−2​d2m,\displaystyle\geq\left(\frac{r}{m}\right)^{d}-\frac{2d^{2}}{m},

where the first inequality is due to ∏i=0d−1(1−xi)≥1−∑i=0d−1xi\prod_{i=0}^{d-1}(1-x_{i})\geq 1-\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}x_{i} for all xi∈[0,1]x_{i}\in[0,1], the second inequality is due to m−i≥m−dm-i\geq m-d for all i∈[d−1]i\in[d-1], the third inequality is due to rm≤1\frac{r}{m}\leq 1 and the fourth inequality is because d≤md\leq\sqrt{m}, so mm−d≤mm−m=11−1/m≤4\frac{m}{m-d}\leq\frac{m}{m-\sqrt{m}}=\frac{1}{1-1/\sqrt{m}}\leq 4 for all m≥2​d2≥2m\geq 2d^{2}\geq 2. ∎

In the following lemma we solve the main differential equation.

Lemma 15.

The unique solution of y′​(t)=(1−n​dm⋅y⁡(t))dy^{\prime}(t)=\left(1-\frac{nd}{m}\cdot y(t)\right)^{d} with initial condition y⁡(0)=0y(0)=0 is y⁡(t)=mn​d⋅(1−(1+n​d​(d−1)m⋅t)−1d−1)y(t)=\frac{m}{nd}\cdot\left(1-\left(1+\frac{nd(d-1)}{m}\cdot t\right)^{-\frac{1}{d-1}}\right).

Proof.

We rewrite the differential equation in the following form:

y′​(t)(1−n​dm⋅y⁡(t))d=1,y⁡(0)=0.\displaystyle\frac{y^{\prime}(t)}{\left(1-\frac{nd}{m}\cdot y(t)\right)^{d}}=1,\ y(0)=0. (1)

By integrating both sides of Equation (1) in [0,t][0,t] we have:

(1−n​dm​y​(t))−(d−1)n​d​(d−1)m−1n​d​(d−1)m=t.\displaystyle\frac{\left(1-\frac{nd}{m}y(t)\right)^{-(d-1)}}{\frac{nd(d-1)}{m}}-\frac{1}{\frac{nd(d-1)}{m}}=t.

We obtain the statement by solving for y⁡(t)y(t). ∎

B.1.2 Differential Equation Method

Lemma 16 (Theorem 2 in [30]).

Given integers a,n≥1a,n\geq 1, a bounded domain 𝒟⊆ℝa+1\mathcal{D}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{a+1}, functions (Fk)1≤k≤a(F_{k})_{1\leq k\leq a} with Fk:𝒟→ℝF_{k}:\mathcal{D}\to\mathbb{R}, and σ\sigma-fields ℱ0⊆ℱ1⊆⋯\mathcal{F}_{0}\subseteq\mathcal{F}_{1}\subseteq\cdots, suppose that the random variables ((Yk​(i))1≤k≤a𝐶𝐿𝑂𝑆𝐸((Y_{k}(i))_{1\leq k\leq a} are ℱi\mathcal{F}_{i}-measurable for i≥0i\geq 0. Furthermore, assume that, for all i≥0i\geq 0 and 1≤k≤a1\leq k\leq a, the following conditions hold whenever (i/n,Y1​(i)/n,…,Ya​(i)/n)∈𝒟(i/n,Y_{1}(i)/n,...,Y_{a}(i)/n)\in\mathcal{D}:

    |𝔼⁡(Yk​(i+1)−Yk​(i)∣ℱi)−Fk​(i/n,Y1​(i)/n,…,Ya​(i)/n)|≤δ\bigl|\E\left(Y_{k}(i+1)-Y_{k}(i)\mid\mathcal{F}_{i}\right)-F_{k}\left(i/n,Y_{1}(i)/n,...,Y_{a}(i)/n\right)\bigr|\leq\delta, where the function FkF_{k} is LL-Lipschitz-continuous on 𝒟\mathcal{D} (the ‘Trend hypothesis’ and ‘Lipschitz hypothesis’),

  2. (ii)

and that the following condition holds initially:

  1. (iii)

    max1≤k≤a⁡|Yk​(0)−y^k​n|≤λ​n\max_{1\leq k\leq a}\bigl|Y_{k}(0)-\hat{y}_{k}n\bigr|\leq\lambda n for some (0,y^1,…,y^a)∈𝒟(0,\hat{y}_{1},\ldots,\hat{y}_{a})\in\mathcal{D} (the ‘Initial condition’).

Then there are R=R⁡(𝒟,(Fk)1≤k≤a,L)∈[1,∞)R=R(\mathcal{D},(F_{k})_{1\leq k\leq a},L)\in[1,\infty) and T=T⁡(𝒟)∈(0,∞)T=T(\mathcal{D})\in(0,\infty) such that, whenever λ≥δ​min⁡{T,L−1}+R/n\lambda\geq\delta\min\{T,L^{-1}\}+R/n, with probability at least 1−2ae−nλ2/(8Tβ2)1-2ae^{-n\lambda^{2}/(8T\beta^{2})} we have

max0≤i≤σ​n⁡max1≤k≤a​|Yk​(i)−yk​(in)​n|< 3​eL​T​λ​n,\max_{0\leq i\leq\sigma n}\max_{1\leq k\leq a}\bigl|Y_{k}(i)-y_{k}\left(\tfrac{i}{n}\right)n\bigr|\;<\;3e^{LT}\lambda n, (1)

where (yk​(t))1≤k≤a(y_{k}(t))_{1\leq k\leq a} is the unique solution to the system of differential equations

yk′​(t)=Fk​(t,y1​(t),…,ya​(t)) with yk​(0)=y^kfor 1≤k≤a,y^{\prime}_{k}(t)=F_{k}\left(t,y_{1}(t),\ldots,y_{a}(t)\right)\quad\text{ with }\quad y_{k}(0)=\hat{y}_{k}\qquad\text{for~$1\leq k\leq a$,} (2)

and σ=σ⁡(y^1,…​y^a)∈[0,T]\sigma=\sigma(\hat{y}_{1},\ldots\hat{y}_{a})\in[0,T] is any choice of σ≥0\sigma\geq 0 with the property that (t,y1​(t),…​ya​(t))(t,y_{1}(t),\ldots y_{a}(t)) has ℓ∞\ell^{\infty}-distance at least 3​eL​T​λ3e^{LT}\lambda from the boundary of 𝒟\mathcal{D} for all t∈[0,σ)t\in[0,\sigma).

B.2 Fixed Set Lower Bound

We proceed to show that Greedy achieves higher value than the fixed set of the kk nodes with the highest degrees, HkH_{k}. First, we calculate the expected value of this set.

Lemma 17.

Let m,n∈ℕm,n\in\mathbbm{N}, m≥d1≥⋯≥dn≥0,k∈[n]m\geq d_{1}\geq\dots\geq d_{n}\geq 0,k\in[n] and draw bipartite graph ℬ=(L,R,ℰ)\mathcal{B}=(L,R,\mathcal{E}) from random model GenR​(n,m,d1,…,dn)\textsc{GenR}(n,m,d_{1},\dots,d_{n}). Then 𝔼⁡[|N⁡(Hk)|]=(1−∏i=1k(1−dim))⋅m≥(1−e−∑i=1kdim)⋅m\E[|N(H_{k})|]=\left(1-\prod_{i=1}^{k}\left(1-\frac{d_{i}}{m}\right)\right)\cdot m\geq\left(1-e^{-\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{k}d_{i}}{m}}\right)\cdot m.

Proof.

Notice that HkH_{k} covers node vjv_{j} as long as at least one of its nodes covers vjv_{j}, so for all j∈[m]j\in[m]:

Pr[vj∈N(Hk)]=1−∏ui∈Hk(1−Pr[vj∈N(ui)])=1−∏i=1k(1−dim)≥1−e−∑i=1kdim.\displaystyle\Pr\left[v_{j}\in N(H_{k})\right]=1-\prod_{u_{i}\in H_{k}}{\left(1-\Pr\left[v_{j}\in N(u_{i})\right]\right)}=1-\prod_{i=1}^{k}{\left(1-\frac{d_{i}}{m}\right)}\geq 1-e^{-\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{k}d_{i}}{m}}.

We have that:

𝔼[|N(Hk)|]=𝔼[∑j∈[m]𝟙{vj∈N(Hk)}]=∑j∈[m]Pr[vj∈N(Hk)]=Pr[v1∈N(Hk)]⋅m,\displaystyle\E\left[|N(H_{k})|\right]=\E\left[\sum_{j\in[m]}{\mathbbm{1}\{v_{j}\in N(H_{k})\}}\right]=\sum_{j\in[m]}{\Pr[v_{j}\in N(H_{k})]}=\Pr\left[v_{1}\in N(H_{k})\right]\cdot m,

where the first equality is by definition, the second equality is by linearity of expectation and the third equality because the probabilities are equal for all j∈[m]j\in[m]. Then the statement follows. ∎

We introduce notation that is useful for the proofs in this section. Informally, Mt​(S)M_{t}(S) is the set of the tt nodes with the highest marginal contributions to a set of nodes SS. Let S⊆LS\subseteq L and define:

u(i)={arg⁡max⁡{|N⁡(u)∖N⁡(S)|:u∈L∖S} if ​i=1arg⁡max⁡{|N⁡(u)∖N⁡(S)|:u∈L∖(S∪{u(1),…,u(i−1)})} otherwise ,\displaystyle u^{(i)}=\begin{cases}\arg\max\{|N(u)\setminus N(S)|:u\in L\setminus S\}&\text{ if }i=1\\ \arg\max\{|N(u)\setminus N(S)|:u\in L\setminus\left(S\cup\{u^{(1)},\dots,u^{(i-1)}\}\right)\}&\text{ otherwise }\end{cases},

where we abuse notation so that arg⁡max\arg\max breaks ties like Greedy, which uniquely defines u(i)u^{(i)}. Then we define Mt​(S)={u(1),u(2),…,u(t)}M_{t}(S)=\{u^{(1)},u^{(2)},\dots,u^{(t)}\}. Now we define the hybrid algorithm:

Yt=Gt∪Mk−t​(Gt).\displaystyle Y^{t}=G_{t}\cup M_{k-t}(G_{t}).

Notice that Yk=GkY^{k}=G_{k} while Y0=HkY^{0}=H_{k}.

𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒢k)|]=𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒴k)|]≥𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒴k−1)|]≥⋯≥𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒴0)|]=𝔼⁡[|N⁡(Hk)|],\displaystyle\E[|N(\mathcal{G}_{k})|]=\E[|N(\mathcal{Y}^{k})|]\geq\E[|N(\mathcal{Y}^{k-1})|]\geq\dots\geq\E[|N(\mathcal{Y}^{0})|]=\E[|N(H_{k})|],
