≥|T|+𝔼⁡[|⋃ℓ=1k−tYℓ|∣ℰ∈ℱ]\displaystyle\geq|T|+\E[|\bigcup_{\ell=1}^{k-t}{Y_{\ell}}|\mid\mathcal{E}\in\mathscr{F}]
=𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒢t)|∣ℰ∈ℱ]+𝔼⁡[|⋃ℓ=1k−tYℓ|∣ℰ∈ℱ]\displaystyle=\E[|N(\mathcal{G}_{t})|\mid\mathcal{E}\in\mathscr{F}]+\E[|\bigcup_{\ell=1}^{k-t}{Y_{\ell}}|\mid\mathcal{E}\in\mathscr{F}]
=𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒴t−1)|∣ℰ∈ℱ],\displaystyle=\E[|N(\mathcal{Y}^{t-1})|\mid\mathcal{E}\in\mathscr{F}],

where the first line is due to Equation (1), the second line is by definition of ℱ\mathscr{F}, the third line is due to Equation (3), the fourth line is by definition of ℱ\mathscr{F} and the fifth line is due to Equation (2). Since the claim holds for any A,T,(Di)i:ui∈L∖AA,T,(D_{i})_{i:u_{i}\in L\setminus A}, it also holds unconditionally. ∎

B.2.1 Structural Lemmas

We show some structural lemmas that help us prove Lemma 18. In this paragraph, when the bipartite graph is clear from context, we use Gt​(E)G_{t}(E) to indicate the output of Greedy when it is run on edge set EE.

Lemma 19 (Uniform marginal contributions).

Let m≥d1≥⋯≥dn≥1m\geq d_{1}\geq\dots\geq d_{n}\geq 1. Draw graph ℬ\mathcal{B} from random model GenR​(n,m,d1,…,dn)\textsc{GenR}(n,m,d_{1},\dots,d_{n}) with edge set ℰ\mathcal{E}. Also define the following arbitrarily:

  1. 1.

    A={a1,…,at}⊆LA=\{a_{1},\dots,a_{t}\}\subseteq L,

  2. 2.

    T⊆RT\subseteq R such that mini⁡di≤|T|≤min⁡{∑i=1tdi,m}\min_{i}{d_{i}}\leq|T|\leq\min\{\sum_{i=1}^{t}d_{i},m\},

  3. 3.

    Di∈[di]D_{i}\in[d_{i}] for all ii such that ui∈L∖Au_{i}\in L\setminus A,

  4. 4.

    ux∈L∖Au_{x}\in L\setminus A.

Let ℱ={E⊆L×R:Gt(E)=A,NE(A)=T,|NE(ui)∖T|=Di∀i s.t. ui∈L∖A}\mathscr{F}=\{E\subseteq L\times R:G_{t}(E)=A,N_{E}(A)=T,|N_{E}(u_{i})\setminus T|=D_{i}\ \forall i\text{ s.t. }u_{i}\in L\setminus A\}. Then we have that:

Pr⁡[Nℰ​(ux)∖T=X∣ℰ∈ℱ]=Pr⁡[Nℰ​(ux)∖T=X′∣ℰ∈ℱ],\displaystyle\Pr\left[N_{\mathcal{E}}(u_{x})\setminus T=X\mid\mathcal{E}\in\mathscr{F}\right]=\Pr\left[N_{\mathcal{E}}(u_{x})\setminus T=X^{\prime}\mid\mathcal{E}\in\mathscr{F}\right],

for any X,X′⊆R∖TX,X^{\prime}\subseteq R\setminus T such that |X|=|X′|=Dx|X|=|X^{\prime}|=D_{x}.

Proof.

Let E1′={ux}×XE^{\prime}_{1}=\{u_{x}\}\times X and E2′={ux}×X′E^{\prime}_{2}=\{u_{x}\}\times X^{\prime}, then we have:

Pr⁡[Nℰ​(ux)∖T=X∣ℰ∈ℱ]\displaystyle\Pr[N_{\mathcal{E}}(u_{x})\setminus T=X\mid\mathcal{E}\in\mathscr{F}] =Pr⁡[ℰ{ux}=E1′∣ℰ∈ℱ]\displaystyle=\Pr[\mathcal{E}_{\{u_{x}\}}=E^{\prime}_{1}\mid\mathcal{E}\in\mathscr{F}]
=Pr⁡[ℰ{ux}=E2′∣ℰ∈ℱ]\displaystyle=\Pr[\mathcal{E}_{\{u_{x}\}}=E^{\prime}_{2}\mid\mathcal{E}\in\mathscr{F}]
=Pr⁡[Nℰ​(ux)∖T=X′∣ℰ∈ℱ],\displaystyle=\Pr[N_{\mathcal{E}}(u_{x})\setminus T=X^{\prime}\mid\mathcal{E}\in\mathscr{F}],

where the first equality is due to ℰ{ux}={(ux,v)∈ℰ:v∈R∖T}\mathcal{E}_{\{u_{x}\}}=\{(u_{x},v)\in\mathcal{E}:v\in R\setminus T\} and E1′={ux}×XE^{\prime}_{1}=\{u_{x}\}\times X so ℰ{x}=E1′\mathcal{E}_{\{x\}}=E^{\prime}_{1} is equivalent to Nℰ​(x)∖T=XN_{\mathcal{E}}(x)\setminus T=X, the second equality is due to Lemma 22 and the third equality is due to ℰ{ux}={(ux,v)∈ℰ:v∈R∖T}\mathcal{E}_{\{u_{x}\}}=\{(u_{x},v)\in\mathcal{E}:v\in R\setminus T\} and E2′={ux}×X′E^{\prime}_{2}=\{u_{x}\}\times X^{\prime} so ℰ{ux}=E2′\mathcal{E}_{\{u_{x}\}}=E^{\prime}_{2} is equivalent to Nℰ​(ux)∖T=X′N_{\mathcal{E}}(u_{x})\setminus T=X^{\prime}. ∎

Lemma 20 (Independent marginal contributions).

Let m≥d1≥⋯≥dn≥1m\geq d_{1}\geq\dots\geq d_{n}\geq 1. Draw graph ℬ\mathcal{B} from random model GenR​(n,m,d1,…,dn)\textsc{GenR}(n,m,d_{1},\dots,d_{n}) with edge set ℰ\mathcal{E}. Also define the following arbitrarily:

  1. 1.

    A={a1,…,at}⊆LA=\{a_{1},\dots,a_{t}\}\subseteq L,

  2. 2.

    T⊆RT\subseteq R such that mini⁡di≤|T|≤min⁡{∑i=1tdi,m}\min_{i}{d_{i}}\leq|T|\leq\min\{\sum_{i=1}^{t}d_{i},m\},

  3. 3.

    Di∈[di]D_{i}\in[d_{i}] for all ii such that ui∈L∖Au_{i}\in L\setminus A,

  4. 4.

    ux,uy∈L∖Au_{x},u_{y}\in L\setminus A.

Let ℱ={E⊆L×R:Gt(E)=A,NE(A)=T,|NE(ui)∖T|=Di∀i s.t. ui∈L∖A}\mathscr{F}=\{E\subseteq L\times R:G_{t}(E)=A,N_{E}(A)=T,|N_{E}(u_{i})\setminus T|=D_{i}\ \forall i\text{ s.t. }u_{i}\in L\setminus A\}. Then we have that:

Pr[Nℰ(ux)∖T=X,Nℰ(uy)∖T=Y∣ℰ∈ℱ]=\displaystyle\Pr[N_{\mathcal{E}}(u_{x})\setminus T=X,N_{\mathcal{E}}(u_{y})\setminus T=Y\mid\mathcal{E}\in\mathscr{F}]= Pr⁡[Nℰ​(ux)∖T=X∣ℰ∈ℱ]\displaystyle\Pr[N_{\mathcal{E}}(u_{x})\setminus T=X\mid\mathcal{E}\in\mathscr{F}]
⋅Pr⁡[Nℰ​(uy)∖T=Y∣ℰ∈ℱ],\displaystyle\cdot\Pr[N_{\mathcal{E}}(u_{y})\setminus T=Y\mid\mathcal{E}\in\mathscr{F}],

for any X,Y⊆R∖TX,Y\subseteq R\setminus T and |X|=Dx,|Y|=Dy|X|=D_{x},|Y|=D_{y}.

Proof.

To obtain the statement we apply Lemma 27 on random sets Nℰ​(ux)∖T,Nℰ​(uy)∖TN_{\mathcal{E}}(u_{x})\setminus T,N_{\mathcal{E}}(u_{y})\setminus T, so it suffices to show the following properties:

  1. 1.

    Pr⁡[Nℰ​(ux)∖T=X∣ℰ∈ℱ]=Pr⁡[Nℰ​(ux)∖T=X′∣ℰ∈ℱ]\Pr[N_{\mathcal{E}}(u_{x})\setminus T=X\mid\mathcal{E}\in\mathscr{F}]=\Pr[N_{\mathcal{E}}(u_{x})\setminus T=X^{\prime}\mid\mathcal{E}\in\mathscr{F}] for any X,X′⊆R∖TX,X^{\prime}\subseteq R\setminus T such that |X|=|X′|=Dx|X|=|X^{\prime}|=D_{x},

  2. 2.

    Pr[Nℰ(ux)∖T=X,Nℰ(uy)∖=Y∣ℰ∈ℱ]=Pr[Nℰ(ux)∖T=X′,Nℰ(uy)∖T=Y∣ℰ∈ℱ]\Pr[N_{\mathcal{E}}(u_{x})\setminus T=X,N_{\mathcal{E}}(u_{y})\setminus=Y\mid\mathcal{E}\in\mathscr{F}]=\Pr[N_{\mathcal{E}}(u_{x})\setminus T=X^{\prime},N_{\mathcal{E}}(u_{y})\setminus T=Y\mid\mathcal{E}\in\mathscr{F}], for any X,X′,Y⊆R∖TX,X^{\prime},Y\subseteq R\setminus T such that |X|=|X′|=Dx|X|=|X^{\prime}|=D_{x} and |Y|=Dy|Y|=D_{y}.

Notice that the first property follows directly from Lemma 19. We proceed to show the second property. Let E1′={ux}×X∪{uy}×YE^{\prime}_{1}=\{u_{x}\}\times X\cup\{u_{y}\}\times Y and E2′={ux}×X′∪{uy}×YE^{\prime}_{2}=\{u_{x}\}\times X^{\prime}\cup\{u_{y}\}\times Y, then we have:

Pr[Nℰ(ux)∖T=X,Nℰ(uy)∖T=Y∣ℰ∈ℱ]\displaystyle\Pr[N_{\mathcal{E}}(u_{x})\setminus T=X,N_{\mathcal{E}}(u_{y})\setminus T=Y\mid\mathcal{E}\in\mathscr{F}] =Pr⁡[ℰ{ux,uy}=E1′∣ℰ∈ℱ]\displaystyle=\Pr[\mathcal{E}_{\{u_{x},u_{y}\}}=E^{\prime}_{1}\mid\mathcal{E}\in\mathscr{F}]
=Pr⁡[ℰ{ux,uy}=E2′∣ℰ∈ℱ]\displaystyle=\Pr[\mathcal{E}_{\{u_{x},u_{y}\}}=E^{\prime}_{2}\mid\mathcal{E}\in\mathscr{F}]
=Pr[Nℰ(ux)∖T=X′,Nℰ(uy)∖T=Y∣ℰ∈ℱ],\displaystyle=\Pr[N_{\mathcal{E}}(u_{x})\setminus T=X^{\prime},N_{\mathcal{E}}(u_{y})\setminus T=Y\mid\mathcal{E}\in\mathscr{F}],

where the first equality is due to ℰ{ux,uy}={(u,v)∈ℰ:u∈{ux,uy},v∈R∖T}\mathcal{E}_{\{u_{x},u_{y}\}}=\{(u,v)\in\mathcal{E}:u\in\{u_{x},u_{y}\},v\in R\setminus T\} and E1′={ux}×X∪{uy}×YE^{\prime}_{1}=\{u_{x}\}\times X\cup\{u_{y}\}\times Y so ℰ{ux,uy}=E1′\mathcal{E}_{\{u_{x},u_{y}\}}=E^{\prime}_{1} is equivalent to Nℰ​(ux)∖T=X,Nℰ​(uy)∖T=YN_{\mathcal{E}}(u_{x})\setminus T=X,N_{\mathcal{E}}(u_{y})\setminus T=Y, the second equality is due to Lemma 22 and the third equality is due to ℰ{ux,uy}={(u,v)∈ℰ:u∈{ux,uy},v∈R∖T}\mathcal{E}_{\{u_{x},u_{y}\}}=\{(u,v)\in\mathcal{E}:u\in\{u_{x},u_{y}\},v\in R\setminus T\} and E2′={ux}×X′∪{uy}×YE^{\prime}_{2}=\{u_{x}\}\times X^{\prime}\cup\{u_{y}\}\times Y so ℰ{ux,uy}=E2′\mathcal{E}_{\{u_{x},u_{y}\}}=E^{\prime}_{2} is equivalent to Nℰ(ux)∖T=X′,∪{uy}×YN_{\mathcal{E}}(u_{x})\setminus T=X^{\prime},\cup\{u_{y}\}\times Y. ∎

Lemma 21.

Let m≥d1≥⋯≥dn≥1m\geq d_{1}\geq\dots\geq d_{n}\geq 1 and ℬ∼GenR​(n,m,d1,…,dn)\mathcal{B}\sim\textsc{GenR}(n,m,d_{1},\dots,d_{n}) with edge set ℰ\mathcal{E}. Also define the following arbitrarily:

  1. 1.

    A={a1,…,at}⊆LA=\{a_{1},\dots,a_{t}\}\subseteq L,

  2. 2.

    T⊆RT\subseteq R such that mini⁡di≤|T|≤min⁡{∑i=1tdi,m}\min_{i}{d_{i}}\leq|T|\leq\min\{\sum_{i=1}^{t}d_{i},m\},

  3. 3.

    Di∈[di]D_{i}\in[d_{i}] for all ii such that ui∈L∖Au_{i}\in L\setminus A,

  4. 4.

    Z⊆L∖AZ\subseteq L\setminus A.

Let ℱ={E⊆L×R:Gt(E)=A,NE(A)=T,|NE(ui)∖T|=Di∀i s.t. ui∈L∖A}\mathscr{F}=\{E\subseteq L\times R:G_{t}(E)=A,N_{E}(A)=T,|N_{E}(u_{i})\setminus T|=D_{i}\ \forall i\text{ s.t. }u_{i}\in L\setminus A\}. Also let ℰZ={(u,v)∈ℰ:u∈Z,v∈R∖T}\mathcal{E}_{Z}=\{(u,v)\in\mathcal{E}:u\in Z,v\in R\setminus T\}. Then we have that:

Pr⁡[ℰZ=E1′∣ℰ∈ℱ]=Pr⁡[ℰZ=E2′∣ℰ∈ℱ],\displaystyle\Pr\left[\mathcal{E}_{Z}=E^{\prime}_{1}\mid\mathcal{E}\in\mathscr{F}\right]=\Pr\left[\mathcal{E}_{Z}=E^{\prime}_{2}\mid\mathcal{E}\in\mathscr{F}\right],

for any E1′,E2′⊆Z×(R∖T)E^{\prime}_{1},E^{\prime}_{2}\subseteq Z\times(R\setminus T) such that |NE1′​(ui)|=|NE2′​(ui)|=Di|N_{E^{\prime}_{1}}(u_{i})|=|N_{E^{\prime}_{2}}(u_{i})|=D_{i} for all ii such that ui∈Zu_{i}\in Z.

Proof.

Let 𝒥={E⊆L×R:NE(A)=T,|NE(ui)∖T|=Di∀i s.t. ui∈L∖A}⊇ℱ\mathscr{J}=\{E\subseteq L\times R:N_{E}(A)=T,|N_{E}(u_{i})\setminus T|=D_{i}\ \forall i\text{ s.t. }u_{i}\in L\setminus A\}\supseteq\mathscr{F}. Also fix an E′∈𝒥E^{\prime}\in\mathscr{J}. Then we have that:

Pr[\displaystyle\Pr[ ℰZ=E1′∣ℰ∈ℱ]=\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{Z}=E^{\prime}_{1}\mid\mathcal{E}\in\mathscr{F}]=
=Pr[ℰZ=E1′∣𝒢t=A,ℰ∈𝒥]\displaystyle=\Pr\left[\mathcal{E}_{Z}=E^{\prime}_{1}\mid\mathcal{G}_{t}=A,\mathcal{E}\in\mathscr{J}\right] (1)
=1Pr⁡[𝒢t=A∣ℰ∈𝒥]⋅Pr[ℰZ=E1′,𝒢t=A∣ℰ∈𝒥]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\Pr\left[\mathcal{G}_{t}=A\mid\mathcal{E}\in\mathscr{J}\right]}\cdot\Pr\left[\mathcal{E}_{Z}=E^{\prime}_{1},\mathcal{G}_{t}=A\mid\mathcal{E}\in\mathscr{J}\right] (2)
=1Pr⁡[𝒢t=A∣ℰ∈ℱ]⋅∑E∈𝒥Pr[ℰZ=E1′,𝒢t=A,ℰ=E∣ℰ∈𝒥]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\Pr\left[\mathcal{G}_{t}=A\mid\mathcal{E}\in\mathscr{F}\right]}\cdot\sum_{E\in\mathscr{J}}\Pr\left[\mathcal{E}_{Z}=E^{\prime}_{1},\mathcal{G}_{t}=A,\mathcal{E}=E\mid\mathcal{E}\in\mathscr{J}\right] (3)
=∑E∈𝒥Pr⁡[ℰ=E∣ℰ∈𝒥]Pr⁡[𝒢t=A∣ℰ∈𝒥]⋅Pr[ℰZ=E1′,𝒢t=A∣ℰ=E]\displaystyle=\sum_{E\in\mathscr{J}}\frac{\Pr\left[\mathcal{E}=E\mid\mathcal{E}\in\mathscr{J}\right]}{\Pr\left[\mathcal{G}_{t}=A\mid\mathcal{E}\in\mathscr{J}\right]}\cdot\Pr\left[\mathcal{E}_{Z}=E^{\prime}_{1},\mathcal{G}_{t}=A\mid\mathcal{E}=E\right] (4)
=∑E∈𝒥Pr[ℰ=E]Pr⁡[𝒢t=A,ℰ∈𝒥]⋅𝟙​{EZ=E1′,Gt​(E)=A}\displaystyle=\sum_{E\in\mathscr{J}}\frac{\Pr\left[\mathcal{E}=E\right]}{\Pr\left[\mathcal{G}_{t}=A,\mathcal{E}\in\mathscr{J}\right]}\cdot\mathbbm{1}\{E_{Z}=E^{\prime}_{1},G_{t}(E)=A\} (5)
=Pr[ℰ=E′]Pr⁡[𝒢t=A,ℰ∈𝒥]⋅∑E∈𝒥:EZ=E1′𝟙{Gt(E)=A}\displaystyle=\frac{\Pr\left[\mathcal{E}=E^{\prime}\right]}{\Pr\left[\mathcal{G}_{t}=A,\mathcal{E}\in\mathscr{J}\right]}\cdot\sum_{E\in\mathscr{J}:E_{Z}=E^{\prime}_{1}}\mathbbm{1}\{G_{t}(E)=A\} (6)
=Pr[ℰ=E′]Pr⁡[𝒢t=A,ℰ∈𝒥]⋅∑E∈𝒥:EZ=E2′𝟙{Gt(E)=A}\displaystyle=\frac{\Pr\left[\mathcal{E}=E^{\prime}\right]}{\Pr\left[\mathcal{G}_{t}=A,\mathcal{E}\in\mathscr{J}\right]}\cdot\sum_{E\in\mathscr{J}:E_{Z}=E^{\prime}_{2}}\mathbbm{1}\{G_{t}(E)=A\} (7)
=Pr⁡[ℰZ=E2′∣ℰ∈ℱ],\displaystyle=\Pr\left[\mathcal{E}_{Z}=E^{\prime}_{2}\mid\mathcal{E}\in\mathscr{F}\right], (8)

where (1) is by definition of 𝒥\mathscr{J}, (2) is by Bayes’ rule, (3) is by law of total probability, (4) is by Bayes’ rule and including the constant in the sum, (5) is due to edges being fixed, therefore the runtime of Greedy is deterministic and using Bayes’ rule on the fraction, (6) is by Lemma 23 which implies that the fraction is constant and can be moved out of the sum, (7) is by Lemma 22 and (8) is by repeating the same steps in reverse. To see why (7) is correct, let edge set E1∈𝒥E_{1}\in\mathscr{J} such that NE1​(ui)∖T=NE1′​(ui)N_{E_{1}}(u_{i})\setminus T=N_{E^{\prime}_{1}}(u_{i}) for all ui∈Zu_{i}\in Z. Also let E2E_{2} be an edge set such that:

NE2​(ui)={(NE1​(ui)∖NE1′​(ui))∪NE2′​(ui)if ​ui∈ZNE1​(ui)otherwise ,\displaystyle N_{E_{2}}(u_{i})=\begin{cases}\left(N_{E_{1}}(u_{i})\setminus N_{E^{\prime}_{1}}(u_{i})\right)\cup N_{E^{\prime}_{2}}(u_{i})&\text{if }u_{i}\in Z\\ N_{E_{1}}(u_{i})&\text{otherwise }\end{cases},

and notice that E2∈𝒥E_{2}\in\mathscr{J} since |NE1′​(ui)|=|NE2′​(ui)|=Di|N_{E^{\prime}_{1}}(u_{i})|=|N_{E^{\prime}_{2}}(u_{i})|=D_{i} for all ii such that ui∈Zu_{i}\in Z. Then by Lemma 22 we have that Gt​(E1)=AG_{t}(E_{1})=A if and only if Gt​(E2)=AG_{t}(E_{2})=A, so summing on both sides we have:

∑E1∈𝒥:NE1​(u)∖T=N1𝟙{Gt(E1)=A}=∑E2∈𝒥:NE2​(u)∖T=N2𝟙{Gt(E2)=A},\displaystyle\sum_{E_{1}\in\mathscr{J}:N_{E_{1}}(u)\setminus T=N_{1}}\mathbbm{1}\{G_{t}(E_{1})=A\}=\sum_{E_{2}\in\mathscr{J}:N_{E_{2}}(u)\setminus T=N_{2}}\mathbbm{1}\{G_{t}(E_{2})=A\},

which suffices by using EE instead of E1,E2E_{1},E_{2} on each sum. ∎

Lemma 22.

Let m≥d1≥⋯≥dn≥1m\geq d_{1}\geq\dots\geq d_{n}\geq 1. Define the following arbitrarily:

  1. 1.

    A={a1,…​ak}⊆LA=\{a_{1},\ldots a_{k}\}\subseteq L,

  2. 2.

    T⊆RT\subseteq R,

  3. 3.

    E′⊆(A×R)∪(L×T)E^{\prime}\subseteq(A\times R)\cup(L\times T) such that NE′​(A)=TN_{E^{\prime}}(A)=T, |NE′​(ui)|=di|N_{E^{\prime}}(u_{i})|=d_{i} for all ii such that ui∈Au_{i}\in A and |NE′​(ui)|≤di|N_{E^{\prime}}(u_{i})|\leq d_{i} for all i∈[n]i\in[n],

  4. 4.

    E1′′,E2′′⊆(L∖A)×(R∖T)E_{1}^{\prime\prime},E_{2}^{\prime\prime}\subseteq(L\setminus A)\times(R\setminus T) such that |NE1′′​(ui)|=|NE2′′​(ui)|=di−|NE′​(ui)∩T||N_{E^{\prime\prime}_{1}}(u_{i})|=|N_{E^{\prime\prime}_{2}}(u_{i})|=d_{i}-|N_{E^{\prime}}(u_{i})\cap T| for all ii such that ui∈L∖Au_{i}\in L\setminus A.

Let B1=(L,R,E1)B_{1}=(L,R,E_{1}) and B2=(L,R,E2)B_{2}=(L,R,E_{2}) be two bipartite graphs such that E1=E′∪E1′′E_{1}=E^{\prime}\cup E^{\prime\prime}_{1} and E2=E′∪E2′′E_{2}=E^{\prime}\cup E^{\prime\prime}_{2}. Then, for all t∈[k]t\in[k], Gt​(E1)={a1,…,at}G_{t}(E_{1})=\{a_{1},\ldots,a_{t}\} if and only if Gt​(E2)={a1,…,at}G_{t}(E_{2})=\{a_{1},\ldots,a_{t}\}.

Proof.

We show by induction that for all t∈[k]t\in[k], if Gt​(E1)={a1,…,at}G_{t}(E_{1})=\{a_{1},\dots,a_{t}\}, then Gt​(E2)={a1,…,at}G_{t}(E_{2})=\{a_{1},\dots,a_{t}\}. The other direction follows by symmetry. For the base case, t=1t=1, we have that by construction of E1,E2E_{1},E_{2}, |NE1​(ui)|=|NE2​(ui)||N_{E_{1}}(u_{i})|=|N_{E_{2}}(u_{i})| for all i∈[n]i\in[n], therefore the algorithm works the same in both graphs and G1​(E1)=G1​(E2)={a1}G_{1}(E_{1})=G_{1}(E_{2})=\{a_{1}\}. For the inductive step, assume towards a contradiction that Gt+1​(E2)={a1,…,at,a}G_{t+1}(E_{2})=\{a_{1},\dots,a_{t},a\} where a≠at+1a\neq a_{t+1}. We consider the two cases in which aa would be chosen instead of at+1a_{t+1}:

  1. 1.

    The marginal contribution of aa was higher than that of at+1a_{t+1}, i.e. |NE2​(a)∖NE2​(Gt​(E2))|>|NE2​(at+1)∖NE2​(Gt​(E2))||N_{E_{2}}(a)\setminus N_{E_{2}}(G_{t}(E_{2}))|>|N_{E_{2}}(a_{t+1})\setminus N_{E_{2}}(G_{t}(E_{2}))|, or

  2. 2.

    The marginal contribution of aa was equal to that of at+1a_{t+1}, but aa was chosen due to the tie-breaking rule.

We proceed to show that the marginal contribution of a,at+1a,a_{t+1} on iteration t+1t+1 is the same regardless of which graph we run Greedy on. The marginal contribution of aa on B2B_{2} is:

|NE2​(a)∖NE2​(Gt​(E2))|\displaystyle|N_{E_{2}}(a)\setminus N_{E_{2}}(G_{t}(E_{2}))| =|NE2​(a)∖NE2​(Gt​(E1))|\displaystyle=|N_{E_{2}}(a)\setminus N_{E_{2}}(G_{t}(E_{1}))|
=|NE2​(a)∖NE1​(Gt​(E1))|\displaystyle=|N_{E_{2}}(a)\setminus N_{E_{1}}(G_{t}(E_{1}))|
=|NE2​(a)|−|NE2​(a)∩NE1​(Gt​(E1))|\displaystyle=|N_{E_{2}}(a)|-|N_{E_{2}}(a)\cap N_{E_{1}}(G_{t}(E_{1}))|
=|NE2​(a)|−|NE1​(a)∩NE1​(Gt​(E1))|\displaystyle=|N_{E_{2}}(a)|-|N_{E_{1}}(a)\cap N_{E_{1}}(G_{t}(E_{1}))|
=|NE1​(a)|−|NE1​(a)∩NE1​(Gt​(E1))|\displaystyle=|N_{E_{1}}(a)|-|N_{E_{1}}(a)\cap N_{E_{1}}(G_{t}(E_{1}))|
=|NE1​(a)∖NE1​(Gt​(E1))|,\displaystyle=|N_{E_{1}}(a)\setminus N_{E_{1}}(G_{t}(E_{1}))|, (1)

where the first equality is by inductive hypothesis Gt​(E1)=Gt​(E2)={a1,…,at}G_{t}(E_{1})=G_{t}(E_{2})=\{a_{1},\dots,a_{t}\}, the second is due to NE1​(ui)=NE′​(ui)=NE2​(ui)N_{E_{1}}(u_{i})=N_{E^{\prime}}(u_{i})=N_{E_{2}}(u_{i}) for all ii such that ui∈Au_{i}\in A therefore NE1​(Gt​(E1))=NE2​(Gt​(E1))N_{E_{1}}(G_{t}(E_{1}))=N_{E_{2}}(G_{t}(E_{1})) because Gt​(E1)⊆AG_{t}(E_{1})\subseteq A, the third is by refactoring, the fourth is due to NE2​(a)∩T={v∈T:(a,v)∈E2}={v∈T:(a,v)∈E′}={v∈T:(a,v)∈E1}=NE1​(a)∩TN_{E_{2}}(a)\cap T=\{v\in T:(a,v)\in E_{2}\}=\{v\in T:(a,v)\in E^{\prime}\}=\{v\in T:(a,v)\in E_{1}\}=N_{E_{1}}(a)\cap T and NE1​(Gt​(E1))⊆TN_{E_{1}}(G_{t}(E_{1}))\subseteq T, the fifth is due to |NE1​(ui)|=|NE2​(ui)||N_{E_{1}}(u_{i})|=|N_{E_{2}}(u_{i})| for all i∈[n]i\in[n] by construction and the sixth by refactoring. The marginal contribution of at+1a_{t+1} on B2B_{2} is:

|NE2​(at+1)∖NE2​(Gt​(E2))|\displaystyle|N_{E_{2}}(a_{t+1})\setminus N_{E_{2}}(G_{t}(E_{2}))| =|NE2​(at+1)∖NE2​(Gt​(E1))|\displaystyle=|N_{E_{2}}(a_{t+1})\setminus N_{E_{2}}(G_{t}(E_{1}))|
=|NE2​(at+1)∖NE1​(Gt​(E1))|\displaystyle=|N_{E_{2}}(a_{t+1})\setminus N_{E_{1}}(G_{t}(E_{1}))|
=|NE1​(at+1)∖NE1​(Gt​(E1))|,\displaystyle=|N_{E_{1}}(a_{t+1})\setminus N_{E_{1}}(G_{t}(E_{1}))|, (2)

where the first equality is by inductive hypothesis Gt​(E1)=Gt​(E2)={a1,…,at}G_{t}(E_{1})=G_{t}(E_{2})=\{a_{1},\dots,a_{t}\}, the second is due to NE1​(ui)=NE′​(ui)=NE2​(ui)N_{E_{1}}(u_{i})=N_{E^{\prime}}(u_{i})=N_{E_{2}}(u_{i}) for all ii such that ui∈Au_{i}\in A therefore NE1​(Gt​(E1))=NE2​(Gt​(E1))N_{E_{1}}(G_{t}(E_{1}))=N_{E_{2}}(G_{t}(E_{1})) because Gt​(E1)⊆AG_{t}(E_{1})\subseteq A, the third is due to NE2​(at+1)∩T={v∈T:(at+1,v)∈E2}={v∈T:(at+1,v)∈E′}={v∈T:(at+1,v)∈E1}=NE1​(at+1)∩TN_{E_{2}}(a_{t+1})\cap T=\{v\in T:(a_{t+1},v)\in E_{2}\}=\{v\in T:(a_{t+1},v)\in E^{\prime}\}=\{v\in T:(a_{t+1},v)\in E_{1}\}=N_{E_{1}}(a_{t+1})\cap T and NE1​(Gt​(E1))⊆TN_{E_{1}}(G_{t}(E_{1}))\subseteq T. We can proceed by considering the two cases. Assume case 1, then by Eqs. 1 and 2 we have that:

|NE1​(a)∖NE1​(Gt​(E1))|>|NE1​(at+1)∖NE1​(Gt​(E1))|,\displaystyle|N_{E_{1}}(a)\setminus N_{E_{1}}(G_{t}(E_{1}))|>|N_{E_{1}}(a_{t+1})\setminus N_{E_{1}}(G_{t}(E_{1}))|,

which is a contradiction since Gt+1​(E1)={a1,…,at,at+1}G_{t+1}(E_{1})=\{a_{1},\dots,a_{t},a_{t+1}\} and Gt​(E1)={a1,…,at}G_{t}(E_{1})=\{a_{1},\dots,a_{t}\} so Gt+1​(E1)∖Gt​(E1)={at+1}G_{t+1}(E_{1})\setminus G_{t}(E_{1})=\{a_{t+1}\}. For case 2, since the tie-breaking rule relies on the order of the nodes of LL and it is the same in both B1,B2B_{1},B_{2}, aa could not be chosen instead of at+1a_{t+1}. Therefore Gt+1​(E2)={a1,…,at+1}G_{t+1}(E_{2})=\{a_{1},\dots,a_{t+1}\}, which concludes the argument. ∎

Lemma 23.

Let Let m≥d1≥⋯≥dn≥1m\geq d_{1}\geq\dots\geq d_{n}\geq 1 and ℬ∼GenR​(n,m,d1,…,dn)\mathcal{B}\sim\textsc{GenR}(n,m,d_{1},\dots,d_{n}) with edge set ℰ\mathcal{E}. Let B1=(L,R,E1)B_{1}=(L,R,E_{1}) and B2=(L,R,E2)B_{2}=(L,R,E_{2}) be two bipartite graphs such that |NE1​(ui)|=|NE2​(ui)|=di|N_{E_{1}}(u_{i})|=|N_{E_{2}}(u_{i})|=d_{i} for all u∈Lu\in L. Then Pr[ℰ=E1]=Pr[ℰ=E2]\Pr[\mathcal{E}=E_{1}]=\Pr[\mathcal{E}=E_{2}].

Proof.

We proceed to show that Pr[ℰ=Ej]=∏i∈[n](mdi)−1\Pr[\mathcal{E}=E_{j}]=\prod_{i\in[n]}\binom{m}{d_{i}}^{-1} for any j∈{1,2}j\in\{1,2\}:

Pr[ℰ=Ei]=Pr[Nℰ(ui)=NEj(ui)∀i∈[n]]=∏i∈[n]Pr[Nℰ(ui)=NEj(ui)]=∏i∈[n](mdi)−1,\displaystyle\Pr[\mathcal{E}=E_{i}]=\Pr[N_{\mathcal{E}}(u_{i})=N_{E_{j}}(u_{i})\ \forall i\in[n]]=\prod_{i\in[n]}{\Pr[N_{\mathcal{E}}(u_{i})=N_{E_{j}}(u_{i})]}=\prod_{i\in[n]}{\binom{m}{d_{i}}^{-1}},

where the first equality is due to ℬ\mathcal{B} being bipartite, the second is due to the nodes of LL selecting neighbors independently and the third is due to each node uiu_{i} selecting did_{i} neighbors uniformly at random from RR. ∎

Lemma 24.

Let Let m≥d1≥⋯≥dn≥1m\geq d_{1}\geq\dots\geq d_{n}\geq 1 and ℬ∼GenR​(n,m,d1,…,dn)\mathcal{B}\sim\textsc{GenR}(n,m,d_{1},\dots,d_{n}) with edge set ℰ\mathcal{E}. Let S={w1,w2,…,wk}⊆LS=\{w_{1},w_{2},\dots,w_{k}\}\subseteq L, then |Nℰ​(S)|≼|Nℰ​(Hk)||N_{\mathcal{E}}(S)|\preccurlyeq|N_{\mathcal{E}}(H_{k})|.

Proof.

Without loss of generality assume that wiw_{i} are in decreasing order of degree |N⁡(wi)||N(w_{i})|. Define the following random sets:

𝒳=Nℰ​(S)=⋃iNℰ​(wi),𝒴=Nℰ​(Hk)=⋃iNℰ​(ui),\displaystyle\mathcal{X}=N_{\mathcal{E}}(S)=\bigcup_{i}N_{\mathcal{E}}(w_{i}),\ \mathcal{Y}=N_{\mathcal{E}}(H_{k})=\bigcup_{i}N_{\mathcal{E}}(u_{i}),

for which we will construct a coupling (𝒳^,𝒴^)(\hat{\mathcal{X}},\hat{\mathcal{Y}}) such that |𝒴^|≥|𝒳^||\hat{\mathcal{Y}}|\geq|\hat{\mathcal{X}}| almost surely. Let 𝒰i⊆R∖Nℰ​(wi)\mathcal{U}_{i}\subseteq R\setminus N_{\mathcal{E}}(w_{i}) be a uniformly random sample of size |Nℰ​(ui)|−|Nℰ​(wi)||N_{\mathcal{E}}(u_{i})|-|N_{\mathcal{E}}(w_{i})| and independent of all other Nℰ​(wj),Nℰ​(uj),𝒰jN_{\mathcal{E}}(w_{j}),N_{\mathcal{E}}(u_{j}),\mathcal{U}_{j} and define:

𝒳^=𝒳,𝒴^=⋃i(Nℰ​(wi)∪𝒰i),\displaystyle\hat{\mathcal{X}}=\mathcal{X},\ \hat{\mathcal{Y}}=\bigcup_{i}\left(N_{\mathcal{E}}(w_{i})\cup\mathcal{U}_{i}\right),

for which it is easy to see that |𝒴^|≥|𝒳^||\hat{\mathcal{Y}}|\geq|\hat{\mathcal{X}}| since by definition of HkH_{k} we have that |Nℰ​(ui)|≥|Nℰ​(wi)||N_{\mathcal{E}}(u_{i})|\geq|N_{\mathcal{E}}(w_{i})|. What remains to show is that (𝒳^,𝒴^)(\hat{\mathcal{X}},\hat{\mathcal{Y}}) is a coupling and it suffices to show that 𝒴^\hat{\mathcal{Y}} is identically distributed to 𝒴\mathcal{Y}. To that end we show the following three properties:

  1. 1.

    Nℰ​(wi)∪𝒰i⟂⟂Nℰ​(wj)∪𝒰jN_{\mathcal{E}}(w_{i})\cup\mathcal{U}_{i}\perp\!\!\!\!\perp N_{\mathcal{E}}(w_{j})\cup\mathcal{U}_{j} for all i≠j∈[k]i\neq j\in[k],

  2. 2.

    |Nℰ​(wi)∪𝒰i|=|Nℰ​(ui)||N_{\mathcal{E}}(w_{i})\cup\mathcal{U}_{i}|=|N_{\mathcal{E}}(u_{i})|,

  3. 3.

    Nℰ​(wi)∪𝒰iN_{\mathcal{E}}(w_{i})\cup\mathcal{U}_{i} is uniformly sampled from RR.

The first property follows by definition since Nℰ​(wi)⟂⟂Nℰ​(wj)N_{\mathcal{E}}(w_{i})\perp\!\!\!\!\perp N_{\mathcal{E}}(w_{j}) and 𝒰i⟂⟂Nℰ​(wj),𝒰j\mathcal{U}_{i}\perp\!\!\!\!\perp N_{\mathcal{E}}(w_{j}),\mathcal{U}_{j} since i≠ji\neq j. The second property also follows by definition since 𝒰i∈R∖Nℰ​(wi)\mathcal{U}_{i}\in R\setminus N_{\mathcal{E}}(w_{i}), therefore |Nℰ​(wi)∪𝒰i|=|Nℰ​(wi)|+|𝒰i|=|Nℰ​(ui)||N_{\mathcal{E}}(w_{i})\cup\mathcal{U}_{i}|=|N_{\mathcal{E}}(w_{i})|+|\mathcal{U}_{i}|=|N_{\mathcal{E}}(u_{i})|. The third property follows from Lemma 25, which concludes the proof. ∎

B.2.2 Probability Lemmas

Lemma 25.

Let 𝒜⊆R\mathcal{A}\subseteq R be uniformly sampled such that |𝒜|=a|\mathcal{A}|=a and ℬ⊆R∖𝒜\mathcal{B}\subseteq R\setminus\mathcal{A} be uniformly sampled such that |ℬ|=b|\mathcal{B}|=b. Then 𝒜∪ℬ\mathcal{A}\cup\mathcal{B} is a uniform (a+b)(a+b)-subset in RR.

Proof.

Let T⊆RT\subseteq R such that |T|=a+b|T|=a+b and we have:

Pr[𝒜∪ℬ=T]\displaystyle\Pr[\mathcal{A}\cup\mathcal{B}=T] =∑N⊆R:|N|=aPr[N∪ℬ=T∣𝒜=N]⋅Pr[𝒜=N]\displaystyle=\sum_{N\subseteq R:|N|=a}\Pr[N\cup\mathcal{B}=T\mid\mathcal{A}=N]\cdot\Pr[\mathcal{A}=N]
=∑N⊆R:|N|=a,|T∖N|=bPr[ℬ=T∖N∣𝒜=N]⋅Pr[𝒜=N]\displaystyle=\sum_{N\subseteq R:|N|=a,|T\setminus N|=b}\Pr[\mathcal{B}=T\setminus N\mid\mathcal{A}=N]\cdot\Pr[\mathcal{A}=N]
=∑N⊆R:|N|=a,|T∖N|=b1(|R|−ab)⋅1(|R|a)\displaystyle=\sum_{N\subseteq R:|N|=a,|T\setminus N|=b}\frac{1}{\binom{|R|-a}{b}}\cdot\frac{1}{\binom{|R|}{a}}
=(b+aa)(|R|a)⋅(|R|−ab)\displaystyle=\frac{\binom{b+a}{a}}{\binom{|R|}{a}\cdot\binom{|R|-a}{b}}
=(b+a)!a!​b!|R|!a!​(|R|−a)!⋅(|R|−a)!b!​(|R|−a−b)!\displaystyle=\frac{\frac{(b+a)!}{a!b!}}{\frac{|R|!}{a!(|R|-a)!}\cdot\frac{(|R|-a)!}{b!(|R|-a-b)!}}
=1(|R|a+b),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\binom{|R|}{a+b}},

where the first equality is due to law of total probability, the second is by definition of ℬ\mathcal{B} and the condition 𝒜=N\mathcal{A}=N which implies that ℬ\mathcal{B} is uniformly sampled from R∖NR\setminus N, the third is by definition of 𝒜,ℬ\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B} as uniformly sampled, the fourth is by counting all the different ways NN can be selected, the fifth is by definition of binomial coefficients and the sixth is by canceling terms in the fraction. ∎

Lemma 26.

Let 𝒜1,…,𝒜n\mathcal{A}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{A}_{n} and ℬ1,…,ℬn\mathcal{B}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{B}_{n} be random subsets of RR such that:

  1. 1.

    𝒜i⟂⟂𝒜j\mathcal{A}_{i}\perp\!\!\!\!\perp\mathcal{A}_{j}, ℬi⟂⟂ℬj\mathcal{B}_{i}\perp\!\!\!\!\perp\mathcal{B}_{j} for all i≠j∈[n]i\neq j\in[n],

  2. 2.

    𝒜i,ℬi\mathcal{A}_{i},\mathcal{B}_{i} uniform in RR for all i∈[n]i\in[n],

  3. 3.

    𝔼⁡[|𝒜i|]≥𝔼⁡[|ℬi|]\E[|\mathcal{A}_{i}|]\geq\E[|\mathcal{B}_{i}|] for all i∈[n]i\in[n].

Then 𝔼⁡[|⋃i=1n𝒜i|]≥𝔼⁡[|⋃i=1nℬi|]\E[|\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{A}_{i}|]\geq\E[|\bigcup_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{B}_{i}|].

Proof.

We start by showing that Assumptions (2), (3) imply higher probability of inclusion for 𝒜i\mathcal{A}_{i} than ℬi\mathcal{B}_{i}. We have that for 𝒳i∈{𝒜i,ℬi}\mathcal{X}_{i}\in\{\mathcal{A}_{i},\mathcal{B}_{i}\} and for any r∈Rr\in R:

Pr[r∈𝒳i]\displaystyle\Pr[r\in\mathcal{X}_{i}] =∑xPr[r∈𝒳i∣|𝒳i|=x]⋅Pr[|𝒳i|=x]\displaystyle=\sum_{x}{\Pr[r\in\mathcal{X}_{i}\mid|\mathcal{X}_{i}|=x]\cdot\Pr[|\mathcal{X}_{i}|=x]}
=∑xx|R|⋅Pr[|𝒳i|=x]\displaystyle=\sum_{x}{\frac{x}{|R|}\cdot\Pr[|\mathcal{X}_{i}|=x]}
=1|R|⋅∑xx⋅Pr[|𝒳i|=x]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|R|}\cdot\sum_{x}{x\cdot\Pr[|\mathcal{X}_{i}|=x]}
=1|R|⋅𝔼⁡[|𝒳i|],\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|R|}\cdot\E[|\mathcal{X}_{i}|], (*)

where the first equality is due to the law of total probability, the second is due to Assumption (2) since 𝒳i\mathcal{X}_{i} is sampling xx elements of RR without replacement, the third is by moving |R||R| out of the sum, and the fourth is by the definition of expectation. So we can show that:

Pr[r∈𝒜i]=1|R|⋅𝔼[|𝒜i|]≥1|R|⋅𝔼[|ℬi|]=Pr[r∈ℬi],\displaystyle\Pr[r\in\mathcal{A}_{i}]=\frac{1}{|R|}\cdot\E[|\mathcal{A}_{i}|]\geq\frac{1}{|R|}\cdot\E[|\mathcal{B}_{i}|]=\Pr[r\in\mathcal{B}_{i}], (2)

where the equalities are due to Equation (1) and the inequality is due to Assumption (3). We can now show that the probability of inclusion in ⋃i𝒜i\bigcup_{i}{\mathcal{A}_{i}} is higher than that of ⋃iℬi\bigcup_{i}{\mathcal{B}_{i}} due to Assumption (1):

Pr[r∈⋃i𝒜i]\displaystyle\Pr[r\in\bigcup_{i}{\mathcal{A}_{i}}] =1−Pr[x∉𝒜i∀i]\displaystyle=1-\Pr[x\notin\mathcal{A}_{i}\ \forall i]
=1−∏i(1−Pr[r∈𝒜i])\displaystyle=1-\prod_{i}{\left(1-\Pr[r\in\mathcal{A}_{i}]\right)}
≥1−∏i(1−Pr[r∈ℬi])\displaystyle\geq 1-\prod_{i}{\left(1-\Pr[r\in\mathcal{B}_{i}]\right)}
=Pr[r∈⋃iℬi],\displaystyle=\Pr[r\in\bigcup_{i}{\mathcal{B}_{i}}], (3)

where the second and third equality is due to independence by Assumption (1) and the inequality is due to Equation (2). Overall we have that:

𝔼[|⋃i𝒜i|]=𝔼[∑r∈R𝟙{r∈⋃i𝒜i]=∑r∈RPr[r∈⋃i𝒜i]≥∑r∈RPr[r∈⋃iℬi]=𝔼[|⋃iℬi],\displaystyle\E[|\bigcup_{i}{\mathcal{A}_{i}}|]=\E[\sum_{r\in R}{\mathbbm{1}\{r\in\bigcup_{i}{\mathcal{A}_{i}}}]=\sum_{r\in R}{\Pr[r\in\bigcup_{i}{\mathcal{A}_{i}}]}\geq\sum_{r\in R}{\Pr[r\in\bigcup_{i}{\mathcal{B}_{i}}]}=\E[|\bigcup_{i}{\mathcal{B}_{i}}],

where the inequality is due to Equation (3). ∎

Lemma 27.

Let 𝒜,ℬ\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B} be random variables with support A,BA,B respectively that have the following properties:

  1. 1.

    Pr[𝒜=a]=Pr[𝒜=a′]\Pr[\mathcal{A}=a]=\Pr[\mathcal{A}=a^{\prime}] for all a,a′∈Aa,a^{\prime}\in A and

  2. 2.

    Pr⁡[𝒜=a,ℬ=b]=Pr⁡[𝒜=a′,ℬ=b]\Pr[\mathcal{A}=a,\mathcal{B}=b]=\Pr[\mathcal{A}=a^{\prime},\mathcal{B}=b] for all a,a′∈Aa,a^{\prime}\in A and all b∈Bb\in B.

Then 𝒜,ℬ\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B} are independent.

Proof.

We proceed to show that Pr[𝒜=a]⋅Pr[ℬ=b]=Pr[𝒜=a,ℬ=b]\Pr[\mathcal{A}=a]\cdot\Pr[\mathcal{B}=b]=\Pr[\mathcal{A}=a,\mathcal{B}=b] for all a∈A,b∈Ba\in A,b\in B:

Pr[𝒜=a]⋅Pr[ℬ=b]\displaystyle\Pr[\mathcal{A}=a]\cdot\Pr[\mathcal{B}=b] =Pr[𝒜=a]⋅∑a′∈APr[𝒜=a′,ℬ=b]\displaystyle=\Pr[\mathcal{A}=a]\cdot\sum_{a^{\prime}\in A}\Pr[\mathcal{A}=a^{\prime},\mathcal{B}=b]
=Pr[𝒜=a]⋅|A|⋅Pr[𝒜=a,ℬ=b]\displaystyle=\Pr[\mathcal{A}=a]\cdot|A|\cdot\Pr[\mathcal{A}=a,\mathcal{B}=b]
=1|A|⋅|A|⋅Pr⁡[𝒜=a,ℬ=b]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|A|}\cdot|A|\cdot\Pr[\mathcal{A}=a,\mathcal{B}=b]
=Pr⁡[𝒜=a,ℬ=b],\displaystyle=\Pr[\mathcal{A}=a,\mathcal{B}=b],

where the first equality is due to law of total probability, the second is due to property (2) and the third is due to property (1) which implies that Pr[𝒜=a]=1|A|\Pr[\mathcal{A}=a]=\frac{1}{|A|}. ∎

B.3 Lower Bound By Concentration Of Opt

Lemma 28.

Let m≥d1≥⋯≥dn≥1m\geq d_{1}\geq\dots\geq d_{n}\geq 1 and ℬ∼GenR​(n,m,d1,…,dn)\mathcal{B}\sim\textsc{GenR}(n,m,d_{1},\dots,d_{n}). For any ϵ∈(0,1)\epsilon\in(0,1), we have that 𝔼[|N(𝒢k)|]≥(1−ϵ)⋅𝔼[|N(𝒪k)|]−m⋅exp(log(nk)−ϵ23(1−e−∑i=1kdi/m)⋅m)\E\left[|N(\mathcal{G}_{k})|\right]\geq(1-\epsilon)\cdot\E\left[|N(\mathcal{O}_{k})|\right]-m\cdot\exp\left(\log\binom{n}{k}-\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{3}\left(1-e^{-\sum_{i=1}^{k}d_{i}/m}\right)\cdot m\right).

Proof.

Let 𝒳={|N(𝒪k)|≤(1+ϵ)⋅𝔼[|N(Hk)|]}\mathcal{X}=\{|N(\mathcal{O}_{k})|\leq(1+\epsilon)\cdot\E\left[|N(H_{k})|\right]\}, then:

𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒪k)|]\displaystyle\E\left[|N(\mathcal{O}_{k})|\right] =𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒪k)||𝒳]⋅Pr⁡[𝒳]+𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒪k)||𝒳¯]⋅Pr⁡[𝒳¯]\displaystyle=\E\left[|N(\mathcal{O}_{k})|\middle|\mathcal{X}\right]\cdot\Pr\left[\mathcal{X}\right]+\E\left[|N(\mathcal{O}_{k})|\middle|\bar{\mathcal{X}}\right]\cdot\Pr\left[\bar{\mathcal{X}}\right]
≤𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒪k)||𝒳]⋅1+m⋅Pr⁡[𝒳¯]\displaystyle\leq\E\left[|N(\mathcal{O}_{k})|\middle|\mathcal{X}\right]\cdot 1+m\cdot\Pr\left[\bar{\mathcal{X}}\right]
=𝔼[|N(𝒪k)|||N(𝒪k)|≤(1+ϵ)⋅𝔼[|N(Hk)|]]+m⋅Pr[|N(𝒪k)|>(1+ϵ)⋅𝔼[|N(Hk)|]]\displaystyle=\E\left[|N(\mathcal{O}_{k})|\middle||N(\mathcal{O}_{k})|\leq(1+\epsilon)\cdot\E\left[|N(H_{k})|\right]\right]+m\cdot\Pr\left[|N(\mathcal{O}_{k})|>(1+\epsilon)\cdot\E\left[|N(H_{k})|\right]\right]
≤(1+ϵ)⋅𝔼⁡[|N⁡(Hk)|]+m⋅exp⁡(log⁡(nk)−ϵ23​𝔼​[|N⁡(Hk)|])\displaystyle\leq(1+\epsilon)\cdot\E\left[|N(H_{k})|\right]+m\cdot\exp\left(\log{\binom{n}{k}}-\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{3}\E\left[|N(H_{k})|\right]\right)
≤(1+ϵ)⋅𝔼[|N(𝒢k)|]+m⋅exp(log(nk)−ϵ23(1−e−∑i=1kdi/m)⋅m),\displaystyle\leq(1+\epsilon)\cdot\E\left[|N(\mathcal{G}_{k})|\right]+m\cdot\exp\left(\log{\binom{n}{k}}-\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{3}\left(1-e^{-\sum_{i=1}^{k}d_{i}/m}\right)\cdot m\right),

where the first line is by tower rule, the second line is due to |N⁡(𝒪k)|≤m|N(\mathcal{O}_{k})|\leq m by Lemma 30, the third line is by definition of 𝒳\mathcal{X}, the fourth line is by Lemma 29 and the fifth line is due to 𝔼⁡[|N⁡(Hk)|]≤𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒢k)|]\E\left[|N(H_{k})|\right]\leq\E\left[|N(\mathcal{G}_{k})|\right] by Lemma 18 and 𝔼[|N(Hk)|]≥(1−e−∑i=1kdim)⋅m\E\left[|N(H_{k})|\right]\geq\left(1-e^{-\sum_{i=1}^{k}\frac{d_{i}}{m}}\right)\cdot m by Lemma 17. Solving for 𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒢k)|]\E\left[|N(\mathcal{G}_{k})|\right] we have that:

𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒢k)|]\displaystyle\E\left[|N(\mathcal{G}_{k})|\right] ≥11+ϵ⋅𝔼[|N(𝒪k)|]−11+ϵm⋅exp(log(nk)−ϵ23(1−e−∑i=1kdi/m)⋅m)\displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{1+\epsilon}\cdot\E\left[|N(\mathcal{O}_{k})|\right]-\frac{1}{1+\epsilon}m\cdot\exp\left(\log{\binom{n}{k}}-\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{3}\left(1-e^{-\sum_{i=1}^{k}d_{i}/m}\right)\cdot m\right)
≥(1−ϵ)⋅𝔼[|N(𝒪k)|]−m⋅exp(log(nk)−ϵ23(1−e−∑i=1kdi/m)⋅m),\displaystyle\geq(1-\epsilon)\cdot\E\left[|N(\mathcal{O}_{k})|\right]-m\cdot\exp\left(\log{\binom{n}{k}}-\frac{\epsilon^{2}}{3}\left(1-e^{-\sum_{i=1}^{k}d_{i}/m}\right)\cdot m\right),

where the second line is due to 1−ϵ≤11+ϵ≤11-\epsilon\leq\frac{1}{1+\epsilon}\leq 1 since ϵ∈(0,1)\epsilon\in(0,1). ∎

Lemma 29.

Let n,m∈ℕn,m\in\mathbbm{N}, m≥d1≥⋯≥dn≥1,k∈[n]m\geq d_{1}\geq\dots\geq d_{n}\geq 1,k\in[n], graph ℬ∼GenR​(n,m,d1,…,dn)\mathcal{B}\sim\textsc{GenR}(n,m,d_{1},\dots,d_{n}). For any δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), n,m,kn,m,k we have that |N⁡(𝒪k)|>(1+δ)​𝔼⁡[|N⁡(Hk)|]|N(\mathcal{O}_{k})|>(1+\delta)\E\left[|N(H_{k})|\right] with probability at most exp⁡(log⁡(nk)−δ23​𝔼⁡[|N⁡(Hk)|])\exp\left(\log{\binom{n}{k}}-\frac{\delta^{2}}{3}\E\left[|N(H_{k})|\right]\right).

≤∑S∈(Lk)Pr[|N(S)|>(1+δ)⋅𝔼[|N(Hk)|]]\displaystyle\leq\sum_{S\in\binom{L}{k}}\Pr\left[|N(S)|>(1+\delta)\cdot\E\left[|N(H_{k})|\right]\right]
≤∑S∈(Lk)Pr[|N(Hk)|>(1+δ)⋅𝔼[|N(Hk)|]]\displaystyle\leq\sum_{S\in\binom{L}{k}}\Pr\left[|N(H_{k})|>(1+\delta)\cdot\E\left[|N(H_{k})|\right]\right]
≤∑S∈(Lk)exp(−δ23⋅𝔼[|N(Hk)|])\displaystyle\leq\sum_{S\in\binom{L}{k}}\exp\left(-\frac{\delta^{2}}{3}\cdot\E\left[|N(H_{k})|\right]\right)
=exp⁡(log⁡(nk)−δ23​𝔼⁡[|N⁡(Hk)|]),\displaystyle=\exp\left(\log{\binom{n}{k}}-\frac{\delta^{2}}{3}\E\left[|N(H_{k})|\right]\right), (2)

where the first line is by definition of 𝒪k\mathcal{O}_{k}, the second line is by union bound, the third line is because |N⁡(S)||N(S)| is dominated by |N⁡(Hk)||N(H_{k})| for all S∈(Lk)S\in\binom{L}{k} by Lemma 24, the fourth line is by Lemma 33 since δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1) by Equation (1) and the fifth line is because |(Lk)|=(nk)=elog⁡(nk)|\binom{L}{k}|=\binom{n}{k}=e^{\log{\binom{n}{k}}}. ∎

Lemma 30.

Let n,m∈ℕn,m\in\mathbbm{N}, m≥d1≥⋯≥dn≥1m\geq d_{1}\geq\dots\geq d_{n}\geq 1 and |N⁡(ui)|=di|N(u_{i})|=d_{i} for all i∈[n]i\in[n]. Then |N⁡(𝒪k)|≤min⁡{∑i=1kdi,|N⁡(L)|,m}|N(\mathcal{O}_{k})|\leq\min\{\sum_{i=1}^{k}{d_{i}},|N(L)|,m\} for any n,m,k,dn,m,k,d.

Proof.

Since the capacity constraint is kk, |N⁡(𝒪k)|≤∑i=1kdi|N(\mathcal{O}_{k})|\leq\sum_{i=1}^{k}d_{i}. Also, since |N⁡(L)||N(L)| is the total value of all the left nodes, |N⁡(𝒪k)|≤|N⁡(L)||N(\mathcal{O}_{k})|\leq|N(L)| and |N⁡(L)|≤m|N(L)|\leq m. ∎

B.3.1 Concentration of HkH_{k}

We define a property that allows us to use Chernoff bounds for sums of variables that are not independent.

Definition 3 (Section 1.10.2.2 in [9]).

Random variables XjX_{j} are negatively correlated if for any choice of I⊆[m]I\subseteq[m] we have

Pr[∀j∈I:Xj=1]\displaystyle\Pr[\forall j\in I:X_{j}=1] ≤∏j∈IPr[Xj=1](1-negative correlation)\displaystyle\leq\prod_{j\in I}{\Pr[X_{j}=1]}\quad\text{(1-negative correlation)}
Pr[∀j∈I:Xj=0]\displaystyle\Pr[\forall j\in I:X_{j}=0] ≤∏j∈IPr[Xj=0](0-negative correlation).\displaystyle\leq\prod_{j\in I}{\Pr[X_{j}=0]}\quad\text{(0-negative correlation)}.

For such variables, the usual Chernoff bounds apply.

Lemma 31 (Theorem 1.10.23 (a) in [9]).

Let X=∑jXjX=\sum_{j}{X_{j}} for X1,…,XmX_{1},\dots,X_{m} identically distributed negatively correlated random variables, such that Xj∈{0,1}X_{j}\in\{0,1\} for all j∈[m]j\in[m]. Then Y=∑i=1mXiY=\sum_{i=1}^{m}X_{i} satisfies the usual Chernoff bound:

Pr[Y≥(1+δ)⋅𝔼[Y]]≤exp(−δ23𝔼[Y]).\displaystyle\Pr[Y\geq(1+\delta)\cdot\E[Y]]\leq\exp\left(-\frac{\delta^{2}}{3}\E[Y]\right).

The following is a useful lemma for showing that variables are negatively correlated.

Lemma 32 (Lemma 1.10.26 of [9]).

Let k,N∈ℕk,N\in\mathbb{N}. For all i∈[k]i\in[k], let ni∈[N]n_{i}\in[N]. Let SS be some set of cardinality NN; for convenience, S=[N]S=[N]. For all i∈[k]i\in[k], let UiU_{i} be a subset of SS having cardinality nin_{i}, uniformly chosen among all such subsets. Let the UiU_{i} be stochastically independent. For all j∈Sj\in S, let XjX_{j} be the indicator random variable for the event that j∈Uij\in U_{i} for some i∈[k]i\in[k]. Then the random variables X1,…,XNX_{1},\dots,X_{N} are negatively correlated.

Finally, we put everything together and show that |N⁡(Hk)||N(H_{k})| admits Chernoff bounds.

Lemma 33.

Let n,m∈ℕn,m\in\mathbbm{N}, m≥d1≥⋯≥dn≥1m\geq d_{1}\geq\dots\geq d_{n}\geq 1, k∈[n]k\in[n] and we draw bipartite graph ℬ=(L,R,ℰ)\mathcal{B}=(L,R,\mathcal{E}) from GenR​(n,m,d1,…,dn)\textsc{GenR}(n,m,d_{1},\dots,d_{n}). Then we have that for all δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1):

Pr[|N(Hk)|>(1+δ)⋅𝔼[|N(Hk)|]]≤exp(−δ23𝔼[|N(Hk)|]).\displaystyle\Pr\left[|N(H_{k})|>(1+\delta)\cdot\E\left[|N(H_{k})|\right]\right]\leq\exp\left(-\frac{\delta^{2}}{3}\E\left[|N(H_{k})|\right]\right).
Proof.

Let Ui=N⁡(ui)U_{i}=N(u_{i}) for all i∈[n]i\in[n], which are independent and uniform in (Rdi)\binom{R}{d_{i}} by definition of the random model. Also let random variables Xj=𝟙{vj∈N(Hk)}=𝟙{vj∈∪i=1kN(ui)}X_{j}=\mathbbm{1}\{v_{j}\in N(H_{k})\}=\mathbbm{1}\{v_{j}\in\cup_{i=1}^{k}N(u_{i})\} for j∈[m]j\in[m]. Then for S=RS=R, ni=din_{i}=d_{i}, N=mN=m, by Lemma 32 we have that X1,…,XmX_{1},\dots,X_{m} are negatively correlated. Then the statement follows by Lemma 31 since |N⁡(Hk)|=∑j=1mXj|N(H_{k})|=\sum_{j=1}^{m}X_{j}. ∎

Appendix D Omitted Proofs Of Section 4

Definition 4 (Erdos-Renyi random graph).

𝔾n,m\mathbbm{G}_{n,m} samples graphs 𝒢=(V,ℰ)\mathcal{G}=(V,\mathcal{E}), with |V|=n|V|=n and ℰ⊆(V2)\mathcal{E}\subseteq\binom{V}{2} chosen uniformly, such that |ℰ|=m|\mathcal{E}|=m.

Definition 5 (Random graph with replacement).

𝔾n,mr\mathbbm{G}^{r}_{n,m} samples graphs 𝒢r=(V,ℰr)\mathcal{G}^{r}=(V,\mathcal{E}^{r}), with |V|=n|V|=n. Also let e1,e2,…,em∈(V2)e_{1},e_{2},\dots,e_{m}\in\binom{V}{2} be independent uniform random samples (with replacement), then ℰr={e1,…,em}\mathcal{E}^{r}=\{e_{1},\dots,e_{m}\}.

Definition 6 (Maximum matching).

Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) and let MM be a maximum matching on GG. We denote the size of this matching as μ⁡(G)=|M|\mu(G)=|M| .

Definition 7 (Maximum matching on random graphs).

Let 𝒢∼𝔾n,m\mathcal{G}\sim\mathbbm{G}_{n,m} and 𝒢r∼𝔾n,mr\mathcal{G}^{r}\sim\mathbbm{G}^{r}_{n,m}. Then μ⁡(n,m)=μ⁡(𝒢)\mu(n,m)=\mu(\mathcal{G}) denotes the size of the maximum matching on 𝒢\mathcal{G} and μr​(n,m)=μ⁡(𝒢r)\mu^{r}(n,m)=\mu(\mathcal{G}^{r}) denotes the size of the maximum matching on 𝒢r\mathcal{G}^{r}.

We state a classic result for the size of maximum matchings in random graphs by [16], but we use the statement of [3]. The difference in some constants is because we assume n=c​mn=cm, while in the original matching setting it was n=c​m/2n=cm/2.

Lemma 39.

[Theorem 4 in [3]] Let n=c​mn=cm for some constant c>0c>0 and sample graph 𝒢\mathcal{G} from 𝔾m,n\mathbbm{G}_{m,n}. Then for any constant ϵ>0\epsilon>0 we have that:

Pr[|μ⁡(m,n)m−(1−γ∗+γ∗+γ∗​γ∗4​c)|≥m−17+ϵ]=o(1),\displaystyle\Pr\left[\middle|\frac{\mu(m,n)}{m}-\left(1-\frac{\gamma^{*}+\gamma_{*}+\gamma^{*}\gamma_{*}}{4c}\right)\middle|\geq m^{-\frac{1}{7}+\epsilon}\right]=o(1),

where γ∗\gamma_{*} is the smallest root of x=2​c​e−2​c​e−xx=2ce^{-2ce^{-x}} and γ∗=2​c​e−γ∗\gamma^{*}=2ce^{-\gamma_{*}}.

The following lemma shows that with high probability there is a sublinear number of pairs of duplicated edges in graphs drawn from model 𝔾n,nr\mathbbm{G}^{r}_{n,n}.

Lemma 40.

Draw 𝒢r​(V,ℰr)∼𝔾n,nr\mathcal{G}^{r}(V,\mathcal{E}^{r})\sim\mathbbm{G}^{r}_{n,n}. Then Pr[n−|ℰr|≥logn]≤1log⁡n\Pr\left[n-|\mathcal{E}^{r}|\geq\log{n}\right]\leq\frac{1}{\log{n}}.

Proof.

Let X=n−|ℰr|X=n-|\mathcal{E}^{r}|, then X≤∑1≤i<j≤n𝟙{ei=ej}X\leq\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq n}\mathbbm{1}\{e_{i}=e_{j}\}, since the right-hand side counts more collisions when the same edge is sampled multiple times. Let i≠ji\neq j arbitrary and we have that:

Pr[ei=ej]\displaystyle\Pr\left[e_{i}=e_{j}\right] =∑{v,v′}∈(V2)Pr⁡[ei={v,v′},ej={v,v′}]\displaystyle=\sum_{\{v,v^{\prime}\}\in\binom{V}{2}}\Pr\left[e_{i}=\{v,v^{\prime}\},e_{j}=\{v,v^{\prime}\}\right]
=∑{v,v′}∈(V2)Pr[ei={v,v′}]⋅Pr[ej={v,v′}]\displaystyle=\sum_{\{v,v^{\prime}\}\in\binom{V}{2}}\Pr\left[e_{i}=\{v,v^{\prime}\}\right]\cdot\Pr\left[e_{j}=\{v,v^{\prime}\}\right]
=(n2)⋅(1(n2))2\displaystyle=\binom{n}{2}\cdot\left(\frac{1}{\binom{n}{2}}\right)^{2}
=1(n2),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\binom{n}{2}}, (1)

where the first line is by law of total probability, the second line is due to independent choice of edges and the third line is because edges are chosen uniformly at random with replacement. For the expectation of XX we have that:

𝔼[X]≤∑1≤i<j≤nPr[ei=ej]=∑1≤i<j≤n1(n2)=(n2)(n2)=1\displaystyle\E[X]\leq\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq n}\Pr\left[e_{i}=e_{j}\right]=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq n}\frac{1}{\binom{n}{2}}=\frac{\binom{n}{2}}{\binom{n}{2}}=1 (2)

where the second equality is by (1). Finally we show the statement:

Pr[X≥logn]≤𝔼⁡[X]log⁡n≤1log⁡n,\displaystyle\Pr\left[X\geq\log{n}\right]\leq\frac{\E[X]}{\log{n}}\leq\frac{1}{\log{n}},

where the first inequality is by Markov and the second is due to (2). ∎

Now we show that the maximum matching size in both random graph models is close.

Lemma 41.

Pr[μr(n,n)≥x]≥Pr[μ(n,n)≥x+logn]⋅(1−1log⁡n)\Pr\left[\mu^{r}(n,n)\geq x\right]\geq\Pr\left[\mu(n,n)\geq x+\log{n}\right]\cdot\left(1-\frac{1}{\log{n}}\right) for all xx.

Proof.

We construct a coupling between 𝔾n,nr\mathbbm{G}^{r}_{n,n} and 𝔾n,n\mathbbm{G}_{n,n} by first sampling 𝒢^r=(V,ℰ^r)∼𝔾n,nr\hat{\mathcal{G}}^{r}=(V,\hat{\mathcal{E}}^{r})\sim\mathbbm{G}^{r}_{n,n} and then sampling an additional n−|ℰ^r|n-|\hat{\mathcal{E}}^{r}| edges from (V2)∖ℰ^r\binom{V}{2}\setminus\hat{\mathcal{E}}^{r} without replacement to obtain 𝒢^n,n=(V,ℰ^)∼𝔾n,n\hat{\mathcal{G}}_{n,n}=(V,\hat{\mathcal{E}})\sim\mathbbm{G}_{n,n}. Then we have that:

Pr[μr(n,n)≥x]\displaystyle\Pr\left[\mu^{r}(n,n)\geq x\right] =Pr[μ(𝒢r^)≥x]\displaystyle=\Pr\left[\mu(\hat{\mathcal{G}^{r}})\geq x\right]
≥Pr[μ(𝒢r^)≥x||ℰ^∖ℰ^r|≤logn]⋅Pr[|ℰ^∖ℰ^r|≤logn]\displaystyle\geq\Pr\left[\mu(\hat{\mathcal{G}^{r}})\geq x\middle||\hat{\mathcal{E}}\setminus\hat{\mathcal{E}}^{r}|\leq\log{n}\right]\cdot\Pr\left[|\hat{\mathcal{E}}\setminus\hat{\mathcal{E}}^{r}|\leq\log{n}\right]
≥Pr⁡[μ⁡(𝒢r^)≥x||ℰ^∖ℰ^r|≤log⁡n]⋅(1−1log⁡n)\displaystyle\geq\Pr\left[\mu(\hat{\mathcal{G}^{r}})\geq x\middle||\hat{\mathcal{E}}\setminus\hat{\mathcal{E}}^{r}|\leq\log{n}\right]\cdot\left(1-\frac{1}{\log{n}}\right)
≥Pr⁡[μ⁡(𝒢^)≥x+log⁡n||ℰ^∖ℰ^r|≤log⁡n]⋅(1−1log⁡n)\displaystyle\geq\Pr\left[\mu(\hat{\mathcal{G}})\geq x+\log{n}\middle||\hat{\mathcal{E}}\setminus\hat{\mathcal{E}}^{r}|\leq\log{n}\right]\cdot\left(1-\frac{1}{\log{n}}\right)
=Pr[μ(𝒢^)≥x+logn]⋅(1−1log⁡n)\displaystyle=\Pr\left[\mu(\hat{\mathcal{G}})\geq x+\log{n}\right]\cdot\left(1-\frac{1}{\log{n}}\right)
=Pr[μ(n,n)≥x+logn]⋅(1−1log⁡n),\displaystyle=\Pr\left[\mu(n,n)\geq x+\log{n}\right]\cdot\left(1-\frac{1}{\log{n}}\right),

where the first line is by definition of 𝒢^r\hat{\mathcal{G}}^{r}, the second line is by law of total probability, the third line is by Lemma 40 since |ℰ^∖ℰ^r|=n−|ℰ^r||\hat{\mathcal{E}}\setminus\hat{\mathcal{E}}^{r}|=n-|\hat{\mathcal{E}}^{r}|, the fourth line is because conditional on |ℰ^∖ℰ^r|≤log⁡n|\hat{\mathcal{E}}\setminus\hat{\mathcal{E}}^{r}|\leq\log{n} we have μ⁡(𝒢^r)≥μ⁡(𝒢^)−log⁡n\mu(\hat{\mathcal{G}}^{r})\geq\mu(\hat{\mathcal{G}})-\log{n}, so μ⁡(𝒢^)≥x+log⁡n\mu(\hat{\mathcal{G}})\geq x+\log{n} implies μ⁡(𝒢r^)≥x\mu(\hat{\mathcal{G}^{r}})\geq x, the fifth line is due to the condition being independent of matching size μ⁡(𝒢^)\mu(\hat{\mathcal{G}}) and the sixth line by definition of 𝒢^\hat{\mathcal{G}}. ∎

Appendix E Generalization to Unbalanced Bipartite Graphs

In this section we generalize Theorem 1 to the case n=O⁡(m)n=O(m). We assume n=c⋅mn=c\cdot m and we show a lower bound for the ratio that decreases as cc increases. Nevertheless, for all constant cc, we obtain a bound that is a constant away from 1−1e1-\frac{1}{e}. Our analysis is very similar to that of Theorem 1, except for the case where the number of left nodes is much smaller than the number of right nodes, i.e. cc much smaller than 11. We use random model ULRR, which we define as follows.

Definition 8.

Let n,m∈ℕn,m\in\mathbbm{N} and d∈[m]d\in[m]. The random model ULRR(n,m,dn,m,d) samples bipartite graphs ℬ=(L,R,ℰ)\mathcal{B}=(L,R,\mathcal{E}) from GenR(n,m,dn,m,d).

In this section we use results from Appendix B, which hold since GenR is a generalization.

Lemma 49.

E.5 Putting Everything Together

Theorem 4.

Let ϵ∈(0,1)\epsilon\in(0,1), m∈ℕm\in\mathbbm{N}, c≥0c\geq 0, n=c​mn=cm, d∈[m],k∈[n]d\in[m],k\in[n] and draw bipartite graph ℬ=(L,R,ℰ)\mathcal{B}=(L,R,\mathcal{E}) from random model ULRR​(n,m,d)\textsc{ULRR}(n,m,d). Then, there exists a positive function f⁡(x,y)f(x,y) that is increasing in xx and decreasing in yy such that 𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒢k)|]≥(1−1e+f⁡(ϵ,c))⋅𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒪k)|]\E\left[|N(\mathcal{G}_{k})|\right]\geq\left(1-\frac{1}{e}+f(\epsilon,c)\right)\cdot\E\left[|N(\mathcal{O}_{k})|\right].

Proof.

Let ϵ=0.3\epsilon=0.3 and m0​(x,y)m_{0}(x,y) be the function from the condition on mm in Lemma 45. For m≥m0​(ϵ,c)m\geq m_{0}(\epsilon,c), the statement follows by Lemmas 42, 43, 44 and 45. For m<m0​(ϵ,c)m<m_{0}(\epsilon,c), the worst-case approximation ratio of greedy is 1−(1−1k)k1-\left(1-\frac{1}{k}\right)^{k}, so we get

1−(1−1k)k≥1−1e+14​e​k≥1−1e+14​e​c​m0​(ϵ,c),\displaystyle 1-\left(1-\frac{1}{k}\right)^{k}\geq 1-\frac{1}{e}+\frac{1}{4ek}\geq 1-\frac{1}{e}+\frac{1}{4ecm_{0}(\epsilon,c)},

where the first inequality is by Claim 2 and the second since k≤n=c​m≤c​m0​(ϵ,c)k\leq n=cm\leq cm_{0}(\epsilon,c). ∎

Appendix F Generalization to Non Regular Bipartite Graphs

In this section, we generalize Theorem 2 to unbalanced, non left-regular bipartite graphs and we use results from Appendix B.

Lemma 50.

=(1−∏i=1k(1−dim))⋅m\displaystyle=\left(1-\prod_{i=1}^{k}\left(1-\frac{d_{i}}{m}\right)\right)\cdot m
≥(1−e−∑i=1kdim)⋅m\displaystyle\geq\left(1-e^{-\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{k}d_{i}}{m}}\right)\cdot m
=1−e−∑i=1kdim∑i=1kdim⋅∑i=1kdi\displaystyle=\frac{1-e^{-\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{k}d_{i}}{m}}}{\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{k}d_{i}}{m}}\cdot\sum_{i=1}^{k}d_{i}

F.3 Main Results

Theorem 5 (Generalization of Theorem 2).

Let n,m∈ℕn,m\in\mathbbm{N} and m≥d1≥d2≥⋯≥dn≥1m\geq d_{1}\geq d_{2}\geq\dots\geq d_{n}\geq 1, arbitrary ϵ∈(0,1)\epsilon\in(0,1) and ℬ∼GenR​(n,m,d1,…,dn)\mathcal{B}\sim\textsc{GenR}(n,m,d_{1},\dots,d_{n}). Suppose that one of the following conditions holds:

  1. 1.

    ∑i=1kdi∉[(ϵ/2)​m,(ϵ/2)−1​m]\sum_{i=1}^{k}d_{i}\not\in[(\epsilon/2)m,(\epsilon/2)^{-1}m] or

  2. 2.

    1k​∑i=1kdi≥204​max⁡(1,(n/m)2)ϵ8\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k}d_{i}\geq\frac{20^{4}\max(1,(n/m)^{2})}{\epsilon^{8}}.

Then greedy achieves, in expectation, a 1−ϵ1-\epsilon approximation.

Proof.

Follows by Lemmas 50 and 51. ∎

Theorem 6 (Power Law Left Degrees).

Let n,m∈ℕn,m\in\mathbbm{N}, X1,X2,…,XnX_{1},X_{2},\dots,X_{n} be i.i.d. samples from Pareto distribution with parameters a>1a>1 and xm​i​n=1x_{min}=1. Also let d1≥⋯≥dnd_{1}\geq\dots\geq d_{n} be their order statistics, ϵ∈(0,1)\epsilon\in(0,1) arbitrary and draw graph ℬ\mathcal{B} from random model GenR​(n,m,⌊d1⌋,…,⌊dn⌋)\textsc{GenR}(n,m,\lfloor d_{1}\rfloor,\dots,\lfloor d_{n}\rfloor). Then 𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒢k)|]≥(1−ϵ−O⁡(1loga⁡m))⋅𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒪k)|]\E\left[|N(\mathcal{G}_{k})|\right]\geq\left(1-\epsilon-O\left(\frac{1}{\log^{a}{m}}\right)\right)\cdot\E[|N(\mathcal{O}_{k})|] for all k≤ϵmn−1/a2​log⁡mk\leq\frac{\epsilon mn^{-1/a}}{2\log{m}}.

Proof.

Let x≥1x\geq 1, then for the highest degree we have that:

Pr[⌊d1⌋≤x]\displaystyle\Pr\left[\lfloor d_{1}\rfloor\leq x\right] ≥⌊d1⌋≤d1Pr[d1≤x]\displaystyle\overset{\lfloor d_{1}\rfloor\leq d_{1}}{\geq}\Pr\left[d_{1}\leq x\right]
=Pr[maxi∈[n]Xi≤x]\displaystyle=\Pr\left[\max_{i\in[n]}X_{i}\leq x\right]
=(Pr[X1≤x])n\displaystyle=\left(\Pr\left[X_{1}\leq x\right]\right)^{n}
=Pareto​(1−x−a)n\displaystyle\overset{\text{Pareto}}{=}\left(1-x^{-a}\right)^{n}
≥Bernoulli​1−n​x−a.\displaystyle\overset{\text{Bernoulli}}{\geq}1-nx^{-a}. (1)

For the sum of the kk highest degrees we have that:

Pr[∑i=1k⌊di⌋≤ϵ​m2]\displaystyle\Pr\left[\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lfloor d_{i}\rfloor\leq\frac{\epsilon m}{2}\right] ≥Pr[k⌊d1⌋≤ϵ​m2]\displaystyle\geq\Pr\left[k\lfloor d_{1}\rfloor\leq\frac{\epsilon m}{2}\right]
=Pr[⌊d1⌋≤ϵ​m2​k]\displaystyle=\Pr\left[\lfloor d_{1}\rfloor\leq\frac{\epsilon m}{2k}\right]
≥Pr[⌊d1⌋≤n1/alogm]\displaystyle\geq\Pr\left[\lfloor d_{1}\rfloor\leq n^{1/a}\log{m}\right]
≥1−n​(n1/a​log⁡m)−a\displaystyle\geq 1-n\left(n^{1/a}\log{m}\right)^{-a}
=1−1loga⁡m,\displaystyle=1-\frac{1}{\log^{a}{m}}, (2)

where the first line is due to ∑i=1k⌊di⌋≤k⁡⌊d1⌋\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lfloor d_{i}\rfloor\leq k\lfloor d_{1}\rfloor, the second line is by dividing by kk, the third line is by assumption k≤ϵmn−1/a/2logmk\leq\epsilon mn^{-1/a}/2\log{m}, the fourth line is by substituting x=n1/a​log⁡m≥1x=n^{1/a}\log{m}\geq 1 for nn large enough into (1) and the fifth line is by rearranging. Then for the value of Greedy we have that:

𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒢k)|]\displaystyle\E\left[|N(\mathcal{G}_{k})|\right] ≥𝔼[|N(𝒢k)||∑i=1k⌊di⌋≤ϵ​m2]⋅Pr[∑i=1k⌊di⌋≤ϵ​m2]\displaystyle\geq\E\left[|N(\mathcal{G}_{k})|\middle|\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lfloor d_{i}\rfloor\leq\frac{\epsilon m}{2}\right]\cdot\Pr\left[\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lfloor d_{i}\rfloor\leq\frac{\epsilon m}{2}\right]
≥(1−ϵ)⋅𝔼⁡[∑i=1k⌊di⌋]⋅(1−1loga⁡m)\displaystyle\geq(1-\epsilon)\cdot\E\left[\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lfloor d_{i}\rfloor\right]\cdot\left(1-\frac{1}{\log^{a}{m}}\right)
≥(1−ϵ−1loga⁡m)⋅𝔼⁡[∑i=1k⌊di⌋]\displaystyle\geq\left(1-\epsilon-\frac{1}{\log^{a}{m}}\right)\cdot\E\left[\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lfloor d_{i}\rfloor\right]
≥(1−ϵ−O⁡(1loga⁡m))⋅𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒪k)|],\displaystyle\geq\left(1-\epsilon-O\left(\frac{1}{\log^{a}{m}}\right)\right)\cdot\E\left[|N(\mathcal{O}_{k})|\right],

where the first line is by tower rule, the second line is by case 1 of Lemma 50 and (2), the third line is due to (1−x)​(1−y)=1−x−y+x​y≥1−x−y(1-x)(1-y)=1-x-y+xy\geq 1-x-y for all x,y≥0x,y\geq 0 and the fourth line is due to 𝔼⁡[∑i=1k⌊di⌋]≥𝔼⁡[|N⁡(𝒪k)|]\E\left[\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lfloor d_{i}\rfloor\right]\geq\E\left[|N(\mathcal{O}_{k})|\right] by Lemma 30. ∎

Our techniques unfortunately do not suffice for extending Theorem 1 to the setting from this section with non left-regular graphs. The main reason is that there are regimes where we only count the number of times we accept nodes whose contribution is the highest possible. But in non left-regular graphs, we could have just one node with a high degree and all other nodes with low degrees, in which case the contribution of the one node is insignificant overall.
